- **A known limit:** cookies are per host name, not per port, so the launcher's and console's
  session cookies are sent to any other service on `localhost` (the Glass, for one). They are
  HttpOnly and eight-hour, and this is a machine the operator owns; recorded, not fixed.

**State of the build after this amendment.** All four decisions are built. **Not done:** a test
against a real Keycloak (the tests use a stand-in that models the refusals); and the harness's
browser end-to-end specs were not run against an enforced console.

### Amendment 3 (29 September 2026): the demo admin also holds the analyst and Studio roles

**Status: Accepted, by the owner's ruling, after signing in as `osprey-demo-admin` and finding no way
to the Ingest Studio.** This supersedes one detail of the second-demo-account decision above, which
kept that account to `osprey-admin` alone so that the analyst account stayed unprivileged and the two
differed in more than name. Nothing else in the record changes.

- **What is decided.** The disposable demo admin (rendered only with `apply --demo-analyst`) holds
  `osprey-admin` and every role the demo analyst holds: `analyst`, `source_author`, `source_approver`
  and `loader`. One demonstration login can therefore open the Admin console, the Glass and the
  Ingest Studio. Its clearance and handling attributes match the analyst's, so the seeded
  investigation is visible to it. The analyst account still does not hold `osprey-admin`.
- **What is not decided or changed.** No role permits anything new. The Conduit still enforces each
  role on each request (ADR-050), and the launcher's tile is still a convenience, not an access
  control. `osprey-admin` did not become a Studio role: that would let every real administrator
  author, approve and load sources, and approve their own, which changes the Studio's separation of
  duties and would need its own record. A real administrator gets only what their organisation's
  provider grants.
- **Why the tile alone was not the answer.** Showing the Ingest Studio tile to an account without a
  Studio role would open a Studio that refuses it at the first step, which reads as a defect.
- **What it costs.** The demonstration no longer shows an account that can administer but cannot
  analyse or approve. `09_INGEST_STUDIO.md` §8 already allows one principal to hold several roles,
  and the analyst account already holds author and approver together, so the demonstration
  already shows one person doing both; this adds administration to that. Where the separation
  matters, sign in as an account that holds one role.
- **On a running Keycloak** the change reaches an existing demo admin by re-running
  `make register-sign-in`, which brings the account's attributes up to the current set. Roles are
  read at sign-in, so the person signs out and in again.

### Amendment 4 (29 September 2026): first run against a real Keycloak, and the sign-in page's look

**What running it found.** The tests use a stand-in identity provider; this was the first time the
work met a real Keycloak, on the owner's deployment. Three things surfaced. None changes a ruling.

- **A custom user attribute is discarded silently unless the realm allows it.** The `roles` claim
  the launcher and the Admin console read is a user attribute. `register-sign-in` created the demo
  admin on a realm where custom attributes were off, so the account signed in with no role and the
  launcher offered only the Glass. `register-sign-in` now switches the setting on first and restores
  the attributes of an account that already exists without them. The stand-in now discards
  attributes as Keycloak does, so the tests can see this.
- **A refused administrator password is the usual sign of two renders disagreeing.** Each `apply`
  writes fresh generated passwords into `deployment.env`; a Keycloak started from an earlier render
  refuses the new one. The error now says so and names the recreate command instead of a bare
  `401`. Keycloak keeps nothing between recreations, so accounts created after its first start do
  not survive one. (Recorded already for the demo analyst; the demo admin is restored by
  `register-sign-in`.)
- **A failed `apply` still rewrites `deployment.env`.** Preflight runs after the files are written,
  so an apply stopped by a busy port or the wrong interpreter leaves new passwords in the file while
  the running stack still has the old ones. Not fixed here; noted so the next operator is not
  surprised.

**Decision: Keycloak's sign-in page is restyled with the design system.** The stock grey page,
under the realm's name in capitals, appeared in the middle of an otherwise designed journey. A login
theme is generated from `apps/workspace/src/design/tokens.css` (the authoritative source: no colour
of its own is introduced, and a test enforces it). `apply` writes it beside the compose file;
compose mounts it into Keycloak **beside** Keycloak's own themes, never over them; the realm names it
and calls itself "OspreyFlow". It extends Keycloak's own login theme, so password reset and error
pages still exist. It changes appearance and wording only. **Nothing about who may sign in or what
they may do is touched.** Like `realm.json` and `litellm.yaml` it is a service's own config, not one
of the deployment's four rendered artefacts. A running Keycloak sees it only after it is recreated
from a compose file that mounts it; `register-sign-in` names the theme in the realm only when
Keycloak lists it, because naming a theme that is absent risks a sign-in page that will not render.

**State of the build after this amendment.** Seen working against a real Keycloak, by the owner in a
browser: sign-in, and the launcher's role-filtered tiles for the demo admin (the Glass and the Admin
console, before Amendment 3's roles reached it). **Not yet seen:** the restyled sign-in page; the
demo admin's Ingest Studio tile; the Admin console opening from the launcher and admitting the
demo admin; the analyst account's view. **Still not done:** the harness's browser end-to-end specs
against an enforced console, and the Docker-backed `apply` test, which has not been run since these
changes. The theme was written against Keycloak 26's sign-in markup without its own stylesheet list
to hand, so it may need a second pass once it has been seen.


## ADR-052 — Who may open a case, and at what level: Author, Editor, Viewer

**Status: Accepted on the owner's rulings of 29 September 2026 for the design as a whole. Four
points are marked "Proposed" and wait for the owner's confirmation. Design only: nothing here is
built.** Until it is built, the current rule (any account in the case's owning unit may do anything to
it) is what the Conduit does, and `03_CONDUIT_MIDDLEWARE.md` §3 still describes it truthfully.

### Context: what was seen

The owner asked that an analyst be shown, before the Glass starts, the cases they have access to
("Fixture vs Enron"), and that an administrator be able to say which analyst has access to which
case, at three levels. Measured on 29 September 2026:

- Access to a case is `owning_unit` only: `InvestigationStore.get_authorized` filters
  `WHERE id = $1 AND owning_unit = $2`. Everyone in the unit is equal on every case, and nobody can be
  made read-only.
- There is no route that lists cases. The Glass therefore cannot offer a choice: it creates a new,
  empty case on every load unless given `?investigation=<id>` (`02_GLASS_FRONTEND.md` §2.1). That is
  why the owner's Glass showed "0 nodes".
- A case has no name, only an identifier, so there is nothing to show in a list.
- 33 routes take a case identifier through `AuthorizedInvestigationDep`, and further stores (sites,
  studio recipes, patterns, alerts, assessments) check ownership of their own records.
- The Conduit has no directory of accounts. Accounts live in the identity provider.
- The real Enron corpus is internal and is never admitted (ADR-035); Fixture Corp is the shippable
  synthetic demo.

### Decision

1. **Three levels, each including the one below it.**
   - **Viewer** browses and queries a case. Nothing they do changes it.
   - **Editor** does everything a Viewer can, and updates the case, adds data to it, and edits the
     settings of its nodes.
   - **Author** does everything an Editor can, and manages access to the case and renames it.
2. **A grant is required, and a grant never widens what an account may see.** A principal opens a
   case only if they hold a level on it. The unit check (`owning_unit`), the clearance check and the
   handling-code filter of ADR-041 still apply on top, unchanged and in the same query. A grant can
   only be made to an account in the case's own unit. The level decides what the account may *do*;
   the existing rules alone decide what it may *see*. A level that does not allow an action is
   refused with the ordinary refusal, and an account with no grant on a case
   receives the same 404 as for a case that does not exist (ADR-041's existence-leak rule, not a 403).
3. **Roles still apply.** A level is necessary, not sufficient: adding data still needs the `loader`
   role, and Studio work its own roles. An Editor without `loader` cannot load.
4. **Who creates and administers.** Whoever creates a case is its first Author. A case's Authors
   manage its access. `osprey-admin` may also manage any case's access as a safety net (so a case
   whose Authors have left is not stranded); that account is **not** thereby able to read the case's
   contents, because reading still needs a level, and the clearance and handling rules are not
   suspended. Every change of access is recorded in the case's history (who, what, to whom, when),
   and cannot be restored away.
5. **Existing cases.** On migration the creator becomes Author and the rest of the unit becomes
   Viewer, until an Author changes it. Because the Conduit has no directory to list "the rest of the
   unit", this is stored as a **unit-wide level on the case** (`viewer` for migrated cases, none for
   new ones), not as one grant per person. An Author may set it to none, viewer or editor.
6. **Cases gain a name.** Required when created (the Glass proposes one), changed by an Author. The
   picker shows names, and never the identifier alone.
7. **The Conduit's surface.** `GET /v1/investigations` lists the cases the caller holds a level on
   (name, their level, counts; nothing the caller may not see). `GET`, `PUT` and `DELETE` on
   `/v1/investigations/{id}/access` read, set and remove grants and the unit-wide level (Author, or
   `osprey-admin`; a Viewer or Editor sees only their own level). Each existing route declares the
   level it needs, and a route with no declared level fails the route-coverage check.
8. **The level each existing route needs.** Read, query and preview routes need Viewer. Routes that
   change the case need Editor. `POST /v1/investigations` needs no grant (the caller becomes Author).
   Access routes need Author. The route-by-route table lives in `03_CONDUIT_MIDDLEWARE.md` §3 once
   built, and the coverage check enforces it.
9. **The Glass** shows a case picker before the workspace opens, listing only cases the account holds
   a level on, and a Share panel for Authors. For a Viewer it hides edit controls; it does not
   enforce anything (ADR-050: the Conduit enforces). Opening `?investigation=<id>` without a level
   shows the ordinary "not found" state.
10. **An Admin console screen for `osprey-admin`** to see and correct access across cases is wanted
    later and is not part of this ADR's first build.

**Proposed, for the owner to confirm** (each is fail-closed until confirmed):

- **P1 — Branching a case** needs Editor on the source, and the caller becomes Author of the copy.
  The alternative, Viewer, lets a read-only account take an editable copy.
- **P2 — Export** (ADR-045, 047) needs Editor as well as its own gates, because it carries data out
  of the boundary. The alternative, Viewer, is looser than the owner's "browse and query".
- **P3 — Naming a grantee.** The Conduit has no account directory, so an Author names the person by
  the account name the identity provider knows them by, and the grant takes effect when that account
  signs in. A mistyped name grants nothing to anyone. A pick-list of accounts needs the identity
  provider's user list and is a separate decision.
- **P4 — Seeding.** The synthetic demos are seeded with the demo analyst as Editor and the demo admin
  as Author, and Fixture Corp is offered by name. The Enron corpus is not seeded and not listed.

### What this does not change

Sign-in (ADR-050, ADR-051), the launcher's tiles (a convenience, not an access control), the clearance
and handling model, the existence-leak rule, and which roles exist.

### Build plan (each stage tests first, with planted faults, and its own commit)

1. Store: names, grants and the unit-wide level; migration; level checks in the authorised-case
   dependency; every route against every level (`route_coverage_check`), including the existence-leak
   404 and that a grant never widens unit, clearance or handling.
2. The listing route and the access routes, with history entries.
3. The Glass picker and Share panel.
4. The seed's grants (P4), and the acceptance rows in `08_ACCEPTANCE_SCENARIOS.md`.

### State of the build

Nothing built. Spec pointers added to `02_GLASS_FRONTEND.md` §2.1 and `03_CONDUIT_MIDDLEWARE.md` §3.

### ADR-052, Amendment 1 (29 September 2026) — the owner's answers to the four proposed points

- **P1 (branching needs Editor on the source) — confirmed.**
- **P2 (export needs Editor, as well as its existing gates) — confirmed.**
- **P3 (an Author names the grantee by account name; a typo grants nothing) — confirmed.**
- **P4 (demo seeding) — not confirmed.** The owner asked for the Enron corpus to be seeded as well.
  That conflicts with the standing rule against admitting a real dataset and with ADR-035, which
  keeps the real corpus `internal` and never seeds it. Nothing has been changed: the seed stays as
  ADR-052 describes it (Fixture Corp, the synthetic Enron-shaped demo, by name; no real corpus) until
  the owner rules on that conflict explicitly. Stage 4 waits on it; stages 1 to 3 do not depend on it.


## ADR-053 — Seeding the real Enron corpus on the owner's own machine only: local, opt-in, never shipped

**Status: Accepted, 29 September 2026, on the owner's explicit ruling. Design only: no loader exists,
no corpus is provisioned and nothing here is built.**

### Context: what was seen

The owner asked, when ADR-052's seeding point was put to them, for the Enron corpus to be seeded
as well as the synthetic demos, and chose to lift the rule against admitting a real dataset "for your
own machine only", provided the corpus stays `internal` and can never enter a shipped build.

What already exists, checked directly rather than assumed:

- ADR-035 §C3 records the owner's own admission of Enron for local development, scale testing and an
  owner-run demonstration on the owner's own secured device, through a local, gitignored list
  (`config/real_data_exceptions.yaml`, managed by `python -m scripts.real_data_exceptions`). Its
  module says plainly that no loader exists yet and that whatever loader is built must call
  `is_permitted()` first and refuse when there is no entry.
- ADR-035 §C1 and §C2: a demo is `shipped` or `internal` (fail-closed), internal datasets are
  provisioned to a gitignored directory named by `OSPREYFLOW_INTERNAL_DEMO_DATA_DIR` and never
  committed, and a packaging gate refuses any artefact that contains one, including inside image
  layers. `.dockerignore` excludes `demo-data/`.
- The deployment's seeds are `hmp`, `fixture-corp` and `scenarios`, all synthetic. There is no Enron
  seed, and the registry (`scripts/demo_registry.py`) has two entries, both synthetic.

### Decision

1. **The rule is lifted for one dataset, on one machine, for the uses ADR-035 §C3 already lists.** It
   is not lifted for any other real dataset, and each of those still needs its own entry and its own
   decision. Nothing in this record changes ADR-035; it builds what §C3 said must be built.
2. **A new seed name, `enron`, is opt-in.** `python -m harness.apply --seed enron` (alone or with the
   others) never runs by default and is never implied by another seed. It refuses, with a sentence
   naming what is missing, unless **all** of these hold:
   - the exceptions list has an entry for the Enron corpus permitting `owner_run_demonstration`
     (checked with `is_permitted()`; the entry names this machine, so a copied checkout on another
     machine is refused);
   - the corpus is present under `OSPREYFLOW_INTERNAL_DEMO_DATA_DIR` (no default, so absence means
     "not provisioned", never a search elsewhere);
   - the seed is being run from a checkout, as the other seeds are (a distributed bundle has no seed
     scripts to run).
3. **The corpus is provisioned by the owner, never fetched by the build or by Claude.** The
   owner places the files under the internal directory. Nothing downloads them, nothing copies them
   into the repository or an image, and the seed reads them in place.
4. **It stays `internal` in the registry.** A third manifest, `distribution: internal`, names its
   paths under `demo-data/`. ADR-035 §C2's packaging gate keeps refusing any artefact containing
   them, and the existing test that reclassifying an internal demo as shipped is still refused
   covers this manifest too. A build that leaves the owner's machine has no Enron seed script in it
   (the seed modules are not in the image), so the opt-in cannot even be attempted there.
5. **Access follows ADR-052.** The seeded case is named for what it is ("Enron corpus (real data,
   this machine only)"), has no unit-wide level, and grants the demo admin Author and the demo
   analyst Editor. It appears in the picker only for an account holding a level on it, and never on a
   deployment where the seed was not run.
6. **The Glass says so when it is not provisioned**, as ADR-035 §C1 already designs: a demo whose
   dataset is absent is shown as unavailable with the reason "dataset not provisioned", not as an
   error. (That display is part of ADR-052's picker stage.)
7. **Tests, named before the code (rule 12).** The seed refuses with no exceptions entry; refuses
   with an entry for another dataset or another use; refuses with an entry but no corpus; refuses
   from a bundle; is never selected by any other seed name; and the registry test proves the
   manifest is `internal` and that flipping it to `shipped` with the data still present is refused by
   the gate. Each is proved to fail by planting the fault it names.

### What this does not change

The rule against real data in the repository and in CI (nothing here is committed or reaches CI, which
has no corpus and no exceptions list), the rule that nothing real is distributed to an attendee, and
the synthetic Fixture Corp, which remains the shippable demo.

### State of the build

Nothing built. The owner has not yet added the exceptions entry or provisioned the corpus; both are
theirs to do on their own machine.


### ADR-052, Amendment 2 (29 September 2026) — P4 settled

**P4 is confirmed as amended.** The demo analyst is Editor and the demo admin is Author on the
seeded demos, Fixture Corp is offered by name, and the real Enron corpus is seeded too, on the
owner's own machine only, opt-in and never shipped, as ADR-053 decides. Stage 4 seeds both.


## ADR-054 — Three folders under one repository: OspreyFlow_Core, OspreyFlow_Build, OspreyFlow_Data

**Status: Accepted in principle on the owner's rulings of 29 September 2026. The layout table below
is proposed and waits for the owner's approval; nothing has been moved.** This is the one exercise for
which the owner lifted the standing rule against restructuring the tree.

### Context: what was seen

The owner asked for the product to be separated from the material that builds and governs it, and
for datasets to have a home of their own. Measured on 29 September 2026:

- 980 tracked files. `tests/` (293), `apps/` (250), `packages/` (195) and `services/` (85) are most.
- The repository already draws this line in one place: `scripts/product_tree_link_check.py` lists
  `process/`, `CLAUDE.md`, `.claude/` and `.graphifyignore` as a private tree that publishable
  documents must not cite. Several large folders (`graphify-out`, `Claude outputs`, `.impeccable`,
  caches) are untracked.
- 412 files outside `spec/`, `tests/` and `process/` cite `spec/` (651 ADR mentions in code and
  docstrings), and 131 cite `process/` or `CLAUDE.md`.
- Eight files in `scripts/` import from `tests/`; four are demo-data generators that the seeds
  call, so the product currently depends on its own test tree.
- Thirty non-test scripts and 45 tests find the repository root from their own location; the
  Makefile, the workflows, `.dockerignore` and the Dockerfiles carry about 210 path references.
- `data/` has no tracked files. It is the Conduit's local analytics store, not a set of datasets.

### Decision

1. **One git repository, whose root is the parent of three sibling folders.** History is kept; files
   move with `git mv`. Nothing is split into a separate repository, and nothing is pushed anywhere
   public.
2. **`OspreyFlow_Core` is the product**: what runs and what is built into an image. It holds no
   dataset and no test. Its Docker build context is the Core folder.
3. **`OspreyFlow_Build` is everything that builds, checks, governs or explains the product**, including
   `spec/`, `tests/` and `process/`, the checks that read them, and the Claude-specific material.
4. **`OspreyFlow_Data` holds datasets, one subfolder per dataset**, plus the Conduit's local runtime
   store in its own subfolder. Core never contains raw data; a deployment finds data through
   `OSPREYFLOW_INTERNAL_DEMO_DATA_DIR`, which now points at this folder. ADR-035 §C1's fixed
   `/demo-data/` is superseded by this location; its rules (internal, never committed, gitignored,
   refused by the packaging gate) are unchanged, and ADR-053's Enron seed reads from
   `OspreyFlow_Data/enron/`.
5. **Citations stay as they are.** `spec/...` and `process/...` in Core files become *logical names*.
   The citation, link and publication checks learn one mapping from a logical name to its new
   location; the 412 and 131 files are not rewritten. The private-tree markers are updated to the new
   locations, and the rule that publishable documents must not cite the private tree is unchanged.
6. **The product does not depend on Build.** The demo-data generators the seeds call (Fixture Corp,
   the HMP fixture, the CDR and seizure fixtures, the scenario cohorts) move into Core as a small
   package, and the tests import them from there. Developer tools that need the test tree
   (`mint_dev_token.py`, `update_golden_baseline.py`) move to Build.
7. **Tests.** The Python suite in `tests/` moves to Build. Unit tests written beside front-end code
   (`*.test.ts(x)` under `apps/`) stay beside it: a test tree cannot be pulled away from the code it
   compiles with without breaking the front-end tooling. Pytest settings move to Build and put Core
   on the import path; CI and `make` run from the parent root.
8. **Root files that must stay at the root** (a tool requires it): `.git`, `.gitignore`,
   `.github/` (GitHub reads workflows only from the repository root), `Makefile` (the one entry point;
   its recipes are repointed), `.claude/` (Claude Code reads its settings and commands from where a
   session opens) and a new one-line `CLAUDE.md` that imports the real one in Build, so a session
   opened at the root or in Build reads the same rules. Everything else Claude-specific moves to
   Build.
9. **Proved, not assumed.** The full test and check suite is run before the move and after each
   commit of it, and must give the same result apart from tests that assert the old paths, which are
   corrected in the same commit. A check that would still pass with a path wrong is proved able to
   fail by planting the fault (rule 12).

### Proposed layout (to be approved)

| Now | Moves to |
|---|---|
| `apps/`, `packages/`, `services/`, `harness/`, `providers/`, `connectors/`, `recipes/`, `deploy/`, `config/`, `osprey.yaml` | `OspreyFlow_Core/` (same names) |
| `pyproject.toml` (dependencies), `uv.lock`, `package.json`, `package-lock.json`, `tsconfig.json`, `eslint.config.js`, `.dockerignore`, `.trivyignore`, `LICENSE`, `NOTICE`, `README.md`, `DEMO_GUIDE.md` | `OspreyFlow_Core/` |
| `scripts/` that run the product: `launch.py`, the four `seed_*.py`, `real_data_exceptions.py`, `demo_registry.py`, `publish_seed.py`, `osprey_bundle.py`, `release_local.py`, `register_tier4_provider.py`, `build_local_basemap.py`, `geo_local_provider.py` | `OspreyFlow_Core/scripts/` |
| Demo-data generators now under `tests/scenarios/fixtures/` | `OspreyFlow_Core/packages/`, as a small package |
| `spec/`, `tests/`, `process/` | `OspreyFlow_Build/` (same names) |
| `scripts/` that check or govern: the `*_check.py` files, `packaging_gate.py`, `licence_check.*`, `doc_site.py`, `simple_markdown.py`, `idp_test_realm.py`, `verify_map.py`, `mint_dev_token.py`, `update_golden_baseline.py` | `OspreyFlow_Build/tools/` |
| `CLAUDE.md` (the real one), `.graphifyignore`, `graphify-out/`, `.impeccable/`, `Claude outputs/`, `dist/`, caches, pytest settings | `OspreyFlow_Build/` |
| `data/` (untracked) | `OspreyFlow_Data/_local-runtime/` (the Conduit's default store path is repointed) |
| `demo-data/` (untracked, where present) | `OspreyFlow_Data/<dataset>/` |
| `.git`, `.gitignore`, `.github/`, `Makefile`, `.claude/`, new one-line `CLAUDE.md` | stay at the root |

Scripts marked uncertain (`doc_site.py`, `simple_markdown.py`, `idp_test_realm.py`, `verify_map.py`,
`publish_seed.py`) are decided by what imports them when the file-level inventory is made; the table
above states the rule, and the inventory states the file.

### Order of work (each step its own commit; the suite run before and after)

1. File-level inventory of every path reference, no moves, for the owner's approval.
2. Data folder and the internal-data path (untracked moves, the environment default).
3. Demo-data generators into Core; tests repointed. No folder moves yet.
4. Build: `spec/`, `tests/`, `process/`, tools, Claude material; the logical-name mapping in the
   checks; pytest settings.
5. Core: the product folders and manifests; Docker contexts, Makefile, workflows, root-finding code.
6. Rebuild the machine-bound pieces (`.venv`, `node_modules`, the generated deployment) and re-run
   the whole suite.

### State of the build

Nothing moved. Case-access stage 1 (ADR-052) starts after step 6.

### ADR-054, Amendment 1 (29 September 2026) — step 4 done: what the Build folder holds and how it is run

`spec/`, `tests/`, `process/`, the checks and the Claude material are in `OspreyFlow_Build/`. Three
points the step settled that the layout table above did not state:

- **Tools run as modules.** Every check is run `PYTHONPATH=OspreyFlow_Build python -m tools.<name>`
  (Makefile and workflows), never as a file path, because a file run that way cannot import the
  shared `tools.layout` that maps logical names to folders. Running them by file path was the
  first thing the Makefile did wrong, and every target failed the same way.
- **Tests run with `-c OspreyFlow_Build/pytest.ini`.** The pytest settings live in Build; the paths
  named to pytest are `OspreyFlow_Build/tests/...`. The coverage check reads both spellings and
  compares on the logical `tests/...`.
- **Tools that move with Build:** `osprey_bundle`, `release_local`, `ci_status_check`,
  `packaging_gate`, `licence_check`, `publish_seed` and the `*_check` files. The seeds, the
  launcher, the registration scripts and anything the running product imports stay in Core's
  `scripts/`. `.dockerignore` names `OspreyFlow_Build` in its private-tree block, as
  `PRIVATE_TREE_MARKERS` now requires.
- **The connector catalogue is found from the code, not the working directory.** `CONNECTORS_DIR`
  looks beside `packages/` first, so a process started from Build (the tests) or Core reads the
  same catalogue; `OSPREY_CONNECTORS_DIR` still overrides.

**State of the build.** Steps 5 (the Core folder) and 6 (machine-bound rebuild) remain.

### ADR-054, Amendment 2 (29 September 2026) — step 5 done: the product is in OspreyFlow_Core

The product folders, manifests (`pyproject.toml`, `uv.lock`, `package.json` and its lock,
`tsconfig.json`, `eslint.config.js`), `LICENSE`, `NOTICE`, `README.md`, `DEMO_GUIDE.md`,
`osprey.yaml` and `.dockerignore` are in `OspreyFlow_Core/`. Points the step settled that the
layout table did not state:

- **The real Makefile is in Core; the root Makefile forwards.** The recipes need the interpreter,
  `node_modules`, `pyproject.toml` and the product's relative paths, all of which are in Core, so
  they run from there (`make -C OspreyFlow_Core`). The root `Makefile` passes every target
  through, so `make launch` from the root and from Core do the same thing. The table's "Makefile
  stays at the root" is amended to say this; `layout.py` maps the logical name `Makefile` to Core.
- **The Docker build context is Core.** Every `context:` and `docker build ... .` is relative to a
  file inside Core, so none changed; `.dockerignore` moved with the context, and `OspreyFlow_Build`
  is still named in its private-tree block as a second line of defence, though a Core context
  cannot contain it. The workflows run from Core (`defaults.run.working-directory`); a step that
  is not a `run` step (the Trivy file scan, the release upload) names its folder itself.
- **The Data folder is Core's sibling**, so the Conduit's default store is
  `../OspreyFlow_Data/_local-runtime/analytics.duckdb`, relative to Core, where the seeds and
  `make` run. A deployment sets `ANALYTICS_DB_PATH` itself and is unaffected.
- **Bundles and other build output go to `OspreyFlow_Build/dist/`**, which `.gitignore` names.
- **Linting the Build folder's `.mjs` checks** runs from Build with Core's ESLint configuration
  (`npm run lint`), because ESLint will not lint outside its own base folder.
- The fallback that let `layout.py` treat the root as Core is gone, and
  `test_no_product_folder_is_left_at_the_root` fails if a product folder is left behind.

**State of the build.** Step 6 (rebuild `.venv`, `node_modules` and the generated deployment inside
Core, and run the whole suite on the owner's machine) remains. `.venv` is still at the root and is
stale: it holds absolute paths.

### ADR-054, Amendment 3 (29 September 2026) — step 6: what was rebuilt here, and what the owner rebuilds

Every check, the fast test subset, `ruff`, `mypy`, `npm run lint`, `npm run typecheck` and
`npm run licence-check` were run against the Core layout from a clean interpreter environment kept
outside the repository. That proves the paths; it does not replace a run on the owner's machine,
because the environment used has no Docker, Keycloak or database and runs Python 3.14.

**Machine-bound and not rebuilt from the sandbox** (an environment built there is for another
operating system and would only mislead): the root `.venv` (stale, holds absolute paths; delete
it), `OspreyFlow_Core/.venv`, and the generated deployment. On the owner's machine:

    rm -rf .venv                              # the stale one at the root
    cd OspreyFlow_Core && uv sync && npm ci   # the interpreter and node_modules, now in Core
    make register-sign-in && make launch      # from the root or from Core; both work

`make ci` (or the full `make test-all`, which needs Docker) is then the whole-suite run.
`OSPREYFLOW_INTERNAL_DEMO_DATA_DIR` still points at `OspreyFlow_Data`; nothing about it changed.

**Left as they were:** an empty `data/` at the root (the old store's shell; delete it) and the
stale `.mypy_cache`, `.pytest_cache` and `.ruff_cache` at the root.

### ADR-054, Amendment 4 (29 September 2026) — OpenStreetMap by default: the tiles folder, the mount and `--tiles-only`

**Seen.** A launched deployment drew no map. Three faults sat behind it, found in order: the
generated deployment mounted nothing at the path a `file://` map provider names, so tiles built on
the host were never visible to the Conduit; the Launch preflight check for the basemap *failed*
once the tiles existed (it looked for the container path on the host), so a successful build
blocked Launch; and the build script always tried to load place names into ArcadeDB, which
`make launch` does not publish, so it stopped with a bare connection error.

**Decided (owner: "option A").**

1. `components.storage.tiles` (default `/var/lib/osprey/tiles`) is the host folder holding the
   built basemap. Every profile mounts it read-only at `/data/tiles` (`TILES_CONTAINER_PATH`) in
   the Conduit. A provider's `source` is a path inside the container; the preflight maps it back
   to the host folder before looking for the file.
2. `build_local_basemap --tiles-only` builds the tiles, registers the provider under the
   container path, and records the tiles folder in the deployment config. It needs no database.
   The place-name load stays a separate step and now explains, in plain words, why it cannot reach
   ArcadeDB and names `--tiles-only`.
3. The preflight passes when the tiles exist behind a `file://` source.

**Not decided.** How the place-name load and the dataset seeds reach ArcadeDB in a launched
deployment (publishing it to 127.0.0.1 only) is an open question for the owner; nothing here
changes that. Also open: the schema allows a blank provider id and a blank default (the Admin
console wrote both to `osprey.yaml`); the proposed class fix is a non-empty rule on both, awaiting
the owner's go-ahead and a reproduction of the console save.

**Tests that fail without this** (each written first and red): in `test_build_local_basemap.py`,
`test_a_tiles_only_build_never_needs_the_database`,
`test_a_provider_can_be_registered_under_the_path_the_conduit_sees`,
`test_the_tiles_folder_is_recorded_without_disturbing_the_rest_of_the_config` and
`test_an_unreachable_database_is_explained_not_dumped_as_a_traceback`;
`test_the_conduit_gets_the_tiles_folder_read_only_where_the_provider_source_points` in
`test_render.py`; `test_the_tiles_folder_has_a_default_and_an_unknown_storage_key_is_still_refused`
in `test_deployment_schema.py`; and in `test_preflight.py`
`test_tiles_that_exist_behind_a_file_url_pass_because_the_conduit_serves_them`,
`test_tiles_in_the_mounted_folder_are_found_where_the_conduit_will_see_them` and
`test_a_missing_tile_file_in_the_mounted_folder_names_the_host_folder`.

### ADR-054, Amendment 5 (29 September 2026) — ArcadeDB published to this machine only; blank map ids refused

**Owner's rulings, 29 September 2026: "Yes" to both.**

1. **ArcadeDB is published on `127.0.0.1` only** (`127.0.0.1:${OSPREY_ARCADEDB_PORT:-2480}:2480`),
   in every profile. The place-name load and the dataset seeds run on the host and need it; the
   launched deployment previously kept it inside Docker, which is why the basemap build could not
   reach it. Bound to loopback, never all interfaces, so it is not reachable from the network.
   The published port joins the Launch port checks through the same override table as the others.
   **Not changed:** the seeds and the build still default to `localhost:2480` and a fixed password;
   the launched deployment generates its own, so they must be pointed at it (a follow-up).
2. **`MapProvider.id` and `MapConfig.default` must be non-empty.** The Admin console had written
   `id: ''` and `default: ''`, which agree with each other, so the consistency check passed them.

**Tests that fail without this:** `test_arcadedb_is_published_to_this_machine_only`
(`test_render.py`); `test_a_provider_with_a_blank_id_is_refused` and
`test_a_blank_default_is_refused_even_when_a_blank_id_would_match_it` (`test_mapconfig.py`).

## ADR-055 — The PaySim mobile-money dataset as an internal demo: what goes in the graph, what goes in the analytics store

**Status: Proposed, 29 September 2026. Three points need the owner's ruling (marked "Owner to rule");
nothing is built. The owner has already ruled: the full set, classified `internal`, and this record.**

### Context: what was seen

The owner asked for PaySim ("Synthetic Financial Datasets For Fraud Detection", Kaggle `ealaxi/paysim1`) to
be built in as a demo dataset. They placed the file at
`OspreyFlow_Data/PaySIM_Dataset/PS_20174392719_1491204439457_log.csv` (Claude cannot download it: Kaggle needs a
login and this machine's network refuses the host). Profiled directly on 29 September 2026:

- **6,362,620 rows, 493,534,783 bytes**, eleven columns: `step`, `type`, `amount`, `nameOrig`,
  `oldbalanceOrg`, `newbalanceOrig`, `nameDest`, `oldbalanceDest`, `newbalanceDest`, `isFraud`,
  `isFlaggedFraud`. `step` runs 1 to 743; one step is one hour, so the set spans about 31 days.
- Types: `CASH_OUT` 2,237,500; `PAYMENT` 2,151,495; `CASH_IN` 1,399,284; `TRANSFER` 532,909; `DEBIT` 41,432.
- **8,213 fraud rows, all `TRANSFER` (4,097) or `CASH_OUT` (4,116); 16 rows flagged by the simulator's own rule.**
- **6,353,307 distinct originating accounts and 2,722,362 distinct destination accounts** (2,150,401 of
  the destinations are merchants, named `M…`; customers are `C…`). Only **9,298** originating accounts
  appear more than once. In graph terms the set is almost entirely disjoint one-edge stars.
- The 8,213 fraud rows touch **16,382 accounts**; the rows touching any of them number **65,676**.

What already exists: `TRANSACTED` (Asset or Endpoint to Asset or Endpoint, directed, temporal) has no
properties; `Endpoint.endpoint_kind` has `iban` and `card` but no account kind; the analytics store holds
events for time-window queries (`load_events`), which is where the HMP incidents live.

### Decision (proposed)

1. **Both stores, split by what each is good at.**
   - **The analytics store takes all 6,362,620 transactions as events**, one event per row, so every
     count, time-window and amount query covers the full set. `step` becomes a timestamp from a fixed,
     declared origin (`step` hours after 2017-01-01T00:00:00Z; the data is simulated and has no real date).
   - **The graph takes the fraud neighbourhood only**: every account that is the origin or destination of
     a fraud row, and every transaction touching one (65,676 rows, of the order of 70,000 nodes). Loading
     all ~8.5 million accounts as nodes would produce a forest with almost no connected structure, cost
     hours and gigabytes, and show an analyst nothing a query cannot. **Owner to rule:** accept this
     split, or require every account in the graph (I recommend the split; the full-graph route is
     buildable but I would want it measured on your machine first).
2. **Mapping.** An account is an `Endpoint` with a new `endpoint_kind` value `account` (customers and
   merchants alike; a merchant carries `M` in its identifier, no separate type). A transaction is a
   `TRANSACTED` edge from origin to destination, with the time from `step`. `TRANSACTED` gains
   properties `amount` (float) and `transaction_type` (enum of the five types). `isFraud` and
   `isFlaggedFraud` are stored as labels on the analytics event, not as edge properties, so a query for
   "what looks fraudulent" can be told apart from "what the simulator says was fraud". **Owner to
   rule:** this is an ontology change (version 9 to 10; recipes pinned to 9 are re-published, as the
   ontology file's own notes describe for every earlier bump). The alternative is no ontology change
   and carrying `amount` and the account kind only in the analytics events (graph edges bare);
   I recommend the change, because an edge with no amount cannot be followed by value.
3. **Classification: `internal`.** A new registry manifest, `distribution: internal`, names
   `OspreyFlow_Data/PaySIM_Dataset/`. The packaging gate already refuses anything under
   `OspreyFlow_Data/`; the registry test that flipping an internal manifest to `shipped` is refused
   covers this one. Nothing is committed, and the seed refuses from a bundle, as ADR-053 does.
4. **Licence.** The simulator is GPL-3.0; the authors ask that E. A. Lopez-Rojas, A. Elmir and
   S. Axelsson, "PaySim: A financial mobile money simulator for fraud detection" (EMSS, Larnaca, 2016)
   be cited. The licence on the Kaggle copy of the data was **not verified** (the page could not be read
   from here); the manifest's `data_licence` is left to the owner to fill from the Kaggle page. Because
   the set is internal and never leaves the machine, nothing is distributed, so the terms do not
   restrict local use; they must be recorded before any change of classification. The seed prints the
   citation.
5. **It is synthetic, so it needs no real-data exception.** ADR-035 §C3's list and ADR-053's
   conditions apply to real datasets. The seed still requires the file under
   `OSPREYFLOW_INTERNAL_DEMO_DATA_DIR` and refuses otherwise, and it is never selected by another seed name.
6. **Access follows ADR-052.** A case named "PaySim mobile money (internal)", demo admin Author, demo
   analyst Editor, no unit-wide level. The Glass shows it as unavailable, "dataset not provisioned", where
   the file is absent.
7. **Tests, named before the code (rule 12).** The reader gives 6,362,620 rows from the real file's own
   first rows (a 12-row fixture with the same columns) and refuses a file with a missing or renamed
   column; the fraud-neighbourhood selection returns exactly the fraud rows' accounts and every row
   touching them on a fixture with a planted second-hop account it must exclude; `step` maps to the declared
   timestamps at both ends (1 and 743); every event carries its `isFraud` label unchanged; the
   registry manifest is `internal` and flipping it is refused; the seed refuses with no file, from a
   bundle, and when another seed name is given. Each is proved to fail by planting the fault it names.

### What this does not change

The synthetic Fixture Corp remains the shippable demo. Nothing here is a claim that PaySim's
accounts are real people: it is simulated data, and the case says so.

### State of the build

Nothing built. Owner to rule on points 1 and 2, then the loader is built tests first.

### ADR-055, Amendment 1 (29 September 2026) — accepted, and what was built

**Owner's ruling: "accept both".** Status is now **Accepted**. Point 1 (analytics store takes every
row; graph takes the fraud neighbourhood only) and point 2 (ontology change: `account` endpoint kind;
`TRANSACTED` gains `amount` and `transaction_type`; version 9 to 10) stand as written.

**Built:** ontology version 10 and the 20 recipe pins moved from 9 to 10; `demo_fixtures/paysim.py`
(reader, neighbourhood selection, `step` mapping, events, graph writes); `scripts/seed_paysim.py`;
the `paysim` registry entry (`internal`, data licence left empty for the owner to record).

**Two decisions made while building, for the owner to overrule:**

1. Graph node and edge identifiers are deterministic (`paysim-acct-<hash of the account name>`,
   `paysim-tx-<hash of the row>`), not ULIDs, and the analytics events use the same ones. That is what
   lets an account selected in the Glass find its events, and lets a second run overwrite rather than
   duplicate. The graph load also refuses if the first account already exists.
2. The graph is written directly, not through a recipe, because the recipe engine's events carry
   only edge properties and the fraud labels must sit on the events, not the edges.

**Not built yet, and stated plainly:** the case "PaySim mobile money (internal)" and its access (ADR-052
stage 1, still queued); the Glass's "dataset not provisioned" state; and a real run. Nothing here has
run against ArcadeDB or the full 6.36 million rows; the tests cover the 11-row fixture, the
refusals and the registry. The first real run is the owner's, and its timing and any ArcadeDB
transaction failures will be recorded here.

**Tests (each proved to fail by planting its fault):** in `tests/scenarios/test_paysim_fixture.py`:
the reader, the missing-column refusal, the fraud neighbourhood, the `step` mapping at both ends, the
labels, the shared identifiers, the graph shape; `tests/demo_registry/test_paysim_manifest.py`;
`tests/test_seed_paysim.py`; `tests/ontology/test_paysim_ontology.py`.

### ADR-052, Amendment 3 (29 September 2026) — stage 1 built

**Built, tests first:** case names, per-account grants, the unit-wide level, the one-off migration and
the access history in `InvestigationStore`; `get_authorized(id, principal, need=...)` with a required
level; every case route (30 HTTP routes, the site routes and the delta stream) declares its level; a
route-level test holds the table (`03_CONDUIT_MIDDLEWARE.md` §3.1) and fails a route with no level.
Verified against a real Postgres for the store and through the real dependency for the routes; the
older route tests' fakes were updated for the new signature.

**Readings I took that the owner may overrule:**

1. `seed`, `expand`, `nodes` (DELETE) and `history/{step}` change the working set, so they need
   **Editor**; only `expand/preview` is Viewer. A Viewer therefore sees a case as saved and can query
   it, but cannot add to it, which follows "nothing they do changes it" strictly. If the owner wants a
   Viewer to explore freely into their own copy, that is a different rule (a branch, which needs Editor).
2. `compute/{metric}` is Viewer (it queries; it does not save).
3. The case name is optional on `POST /v1/investigations` for now (default "Untitled case") so the
   Glass keeps working; it becomes required when the Glass proposes one (stage 3).
4. Other stores keyed to a case or unit (studio recipes, patterns, alerts, assessments) still check
   their own records by unit only; they are not yet level-aware.
5. `alerts/{id}/jump` creates a new case owned by the caller and does not read the source case, so it
   needs no level on it.

**Not yet:** the listing and access routes with the admin safety net (stage 2); the Glass picker and
Share panel (stage 3); the demo seeds' grants and the acceptance rows (stage 4).

### ADR-052, Amendment 4 (29 September 2026) — stage 2 built

**Built, tests first:** `GET /v1/investigations` (the cases the caller holds a level on); `PATCH` to
rename (Author); `GET .../access` (own level for anyone; the unit-wide level and all grants for an
Author only); `PUT .../access` (the unit-wide level: none, Viewer or Editor); `PUT` and `DELETE
.../access/grants/{account}`; `GET .../access/history`. Every change is written to the case's access
history and to the audit stream. Store tests run against a real Postgres; route tests go through the
real level dependencies. Six faults were planted and each is caught (any account treated as
administrator; a Viewer shown the grant list; the list ignoring the unit; a unit-wide Author level;
plus the earlier stage's).

**Two readings for the owner to overrule:**

1. The administrator safety net requires the administrator to be in the case's **own unit**. ADR-052
   §4 says "any case"; the Conduit's unit rule (ADR-041) has no cross-unit exception anywhere, so I
   did not add one for this. An administrator of another unit finds nothing.
2. The unit-wide level is refused as `author`. §5 lists none, viewer and editor; a whole unit being
   Authors would make "who manages access" unanswerable.

**Not yet:** the Glass picker and Share panel (stage 3), with counts in the listing and the case name
becoming required; the demo seeds' grants and the acceptance rows (stage 4).

### ADR-052, Amendment 5 (29 September 2026) — stage 3 built: the picker and the switchers

**Seen:** the owner opened the Glass and got an empty, freshly created case ("Case 01M3PYS1", 0
nodes) with no way to choose the dataset to work on, and no way to choose or create a case from the
Ingest Studio. Cause: the Glass created a case on every load that had no id.

**Built, tests first:** the Glass no longer creates a case on load. With no case chosen it shows a
picker of the cases the caller holds a level on (name and own level), pre-selecting the last case
used in this browser tab, and a "New case" form (a blank name is refused). The header shows the
current case with a switcher. The Ingest Studio shows the same switcher above its tabs, so data is
loaded into a case the analyst has chosen on purpose. Switching reloads the page (the per-case state
is built once). 20 new tests; workspace lint, typecheck and all 297 tests pass.

**Reading for the owner to overrule:** the case name is still optional at the API; the Glass always
sends one. Making it required is a one-line change once you agree.

**Not yet:** the Share panel for Authors and hiding edit controls from Viewers (the Conduit already
refuses them), counts in the listing, and stage 4 (demo grants and acceptance rows).

### ADR-049, Amendment (29 September 2026) — Start brings the deployment up to date

**Seen:** after code changes the Glass, the Conduit and the sign-in page stayed as they were, because
the launcher's Start ran `docker compose up` alone, which never rebuilds an image or rewrites the
mounted sign-in theme. Each fix needed its own command, and restarting Keycloak removed the demo
administrator (Keycloak's database is not persisted) while `deployment.env` still named their
password, so the password appeared to stop working.

**Decision (taken on the owner's request for one start sequence):** the launcher's Start, and
`make refresh`, run `scripts/refresh.py`: write the theme, `docker compose build`, `up -d --wait`,
restart Keycloak only if the theme changed, then register the sign-in accounts again. This replaces
the earlier statement that Start "does not rebuild anything". It still never re-renders the
deployment (new secrets for stores that keep the old ones), never removes a volume, never forces a
recreate and never seeds; first-time set-up stays `python -m harness.apply`. The start grace period
is 900 seconds because a build after a code change takes minutes.

**Named tests:** `tests/test_refresh.py` (order; `deployment.env` unchanged; no `down`, `-v` or
`--force-recreate`; no restart when the theme is unchanged; registration last; a failed registration
names `make register-sign-in`; a failed build starts nothing) and `tests/test_launch.py`. Three
faults were planted (build skipped, restart always, registration skipped); each is caught.

### ADR-049, Amendment 2 (29 September 2026) — the demo analyst is repaired too

**Seen:** after `make refresh` the owner still could not sign in with the password in `deployment.env`.
Cause: the realm document carries no credentials; `apply` sets the demo analyst's password once,
through the admin API, and Keycloak keeps nothing across a restart. Registering the sign-in accounts
(ADR-049 Amendment, ADR-051) repaired only the demo administrator, so the analyst had no password
while the file still named one. Registering now also creates the analyst if absent and sets its
password from `OSPREY_DEMO_ANALYST_PASSWORD`, only when the file names one (a deployment applied
without a demo analyst gets none). No secret is regenerated, printed or rewritten. Named tests:
`tests/harness/test_register_sign_in.py` (restored after an empty restart; each account keeps its
own password; none invented; never printed).

### ADR-052, Amendment 6 (29 September 2026) — the picker on a real deployment

**Seen on the owner's deployment**, four things, each reproduced in a test before it was fixed:

1. Rows in the picker were empty buttons. Cases made before names existed have no name. They are now
   shown as "Untitled case · created <date time UTC>", never an empty button, in the picker and the
   switcher. Named cases are listed first, then untitled ones, newest first within each.
2. Choosing a case showed the sign-in screen. Switching reloads the page (the working set, filters and
   delta stream are built once per case) and the sign-in is held in memory. The Glass now opens a case
   with `?investigation=<id>&from=case` (plus `&view=ingest` from the Ingest Studio), which starts the
   sign-in without a click, exactly as arriving from the launcher does (`auth/launcherHandoff.ts`); it
   grants nothing and the Conduit still checks every request.
3. The cases are empty. The twelve listed were created by the old Glass, which made a blank case on
   every load. Nothing was wrong with them. No dataset has been seeded into a named case yet (stage 4).
4. The 405 on the case list was an API image built before stage 2; fixed by the refresh sequence
   (ADR-049 Amendment).

**Not built, and asked of the owner:** whether to offer clearing out the blank cases (a delete, so an
ADR-052 decision: only an Author, an audited soft delete, never a hard delete) or leave them.

### ADR-052, Amendment 7 (29 September 2026) — removing a case

**Owner's request:** "yes please add the remove button" (for the blank cases the old Glass created).

**Decision:** a **soft remove**. `DELETE /v1/investigations/{id}` sets `removed_at` and `removed_by` on
the case and writes a `remove` line to its access history and the audit stream. Nothing is deleted:
the row, its grants and history, and everything in the graph and analytics stores stay. Every read
(the level lookup, the list, the administrator lookup, the raw lookup) then treats the case as one
that does not exist, the same 404 as an unknown case (ADR-041), so a removed case cannot be told from
one that never existed. A branch of a removed case is unaffected. Removing it twice is a 404.

**Who:** an Author (level table: `DELETE` on a case needs Author). Reading taken, for the owner to
overrule: an `osprey-admin` in the case's **own unit** may also remove it, through the same safety net
as ADR-052 §4, because the blank cases were made by an account no one now holds as Author. It confers
no read access. An administrator of another unit finds nothing.

**In the Glass:** the picker shows "Remove" on cases the account is an Author of, and on every case to
an administrator; it asks once ("Remove this case from every list? Nothing is deleted."), then removes.
A refusal is shown and the case stays listed.

**Not built:** restoring a removed case (an operator can clear `removed_at` in the database; a Glass
"restore" is a further design question), and a hard delete, which this ADR does not offer.

**Named tests:** `tests/services/api/test_investigation_access_store.py` (real Postgres: same
not-found at every level; leaves the list; the record and history stay; twice is not-found; a branch
survives), `test_investigation_access_routes.py` (Author 204, Editor/Viewer 403, no level 404,
administrator of the unit 204, another unit's 404), `test_investigation_levels.py` (the level table).
Two faults were planted (the level lookup and the list each forgetting to skip removed cases); each is
caught. Glass: `CasePicker.test.tsx`, `cases.test.ts`.

### ADR-052, Amendment 8 (29 September 2026) — getting back to the picker

**Seen:** once a case was open there was no way back to the list of cases; the header's case selector is
a drop-down, which does not scale to a dozen cases, and Remove lives only in the picker.

**Built, tests first:** an **All cases** button in the header (beside the case selector and New case)
shows the picker over the open case, with **Back to <case>** to return. It does not reload the page, so
the sign-in and the case's working state are kept. Choosing a different case still reloads (Amendment
6). The Back button is not offered for a case that has just been removed, or when no case is open.
Remove is offered only on cases the account is an Author of, and on every case to an administrator
(Amendment 7); a Viewer or Editor sees no Remove.

### ADR-055, Amendment 2 (30 September 2026) — seeding runs inside the deployment, into a named case

**Why.** The first seed ran on the host and wrote a DuckDB file the deployment never reads: the
analytics store lives in the Docker volume `osprey-data`, and Postgres and ArcadeDB are on an internal
network. It also took a raw `--investigation-scope`, so the case it filled was invisible in the picker.

**Built, tests first:** `scripts/seed_internal.py` (`make seed-paysim`) starts a one-shot container from
the `api` image on the deployment's own network and volume, with the checkout's `scripts/` and the
data folder mounted read-only, and runs the seed there. The seed creates (or reuses, by name) a case
named for the dataset in the demo unit and grants the demo administrator Author and the demo analyst
Editor, so both can open it from the picker (ADR-052). The Conduit is stopped for the run only with
`--stop-api`, because DuckDB takes one writer; it is always started again afterwards, including when
the seed fails. Without the flag, a running Conduit is a refusal that names the flag.

**A reading, for the owner to overrule:** the container has no git checkout, so the seed is given
`--attested-checkout` by the orchestrator, which itself runs from the checkout and refuses to start
unless the data folder is outside the tree (ADR-053). The flag records that reading; it does not
weaken the refusal for a direct host run.

### ADR-052, Amendment 9 (30 September 2026) — seeded cases carry their grants

Seeds create cases through the same access store as the Glass (`scripts/case_seed.py`, `ensure_case`),
not through raw scope strings, so a seeded case appears in the picker with its name and grants. Grants
are given as `--grant <keycloak sub>=<level>` and are applied by the seeding account. The orchestrator
looks the demo accounts' subjects up in Keycloak; if an account is missing it names
`make register-sign-in`. Fixture Corp and HMP have not been created on this machine (the owner did not
run `harness.apply --seed`), so they are loaded the same way, as named, shared cases.

### ADR-053, Amendment 1 (30 September 2026) — the mapping, ruled; the loader built

**Owner's ruling: "Option A and one case for all the 150 mailboxes".** The corpus is one case, not one
per custodian.

**Mapping (option A, with one correction to my own wording).** An email address is an `Endpoint` of
kind `email`; no `Person` is invented from an address (a `Person` needs a family name the corpus does
not give). Each directed sender-to-recipient pair is one summarised `COMMUNICATED_WITH` edge, and each
message to each recipient (To, Cc and Bcc, kept as `kind`) is one analytics event on that edge, with
subject, `Message-ID`, custodian, folder and a 300-character excerpt. **No ontology change** (the
Endpoint kind and the edge already exist). Messages are read once by `Message-ID` (or a hash of the
headers and body when there is none), in a fixed order. Undated, senderless, unreadable and
recipientless messages are counted and reported, never guessed. **The graph takes the company's own
addresses (`@enron.com`) and the links between them; every message, including those to and from
outside addresses, is in the analytics store**, the same split ADR-055 makes for PaySim. The full
bodies are not loaded (over a gigabyte of text on every event), only the excerpt: the owner may rule
otherwise.

**Corrections to ADR-053 as written (by amendment; the ADR is not edited):**

1. Point 4 says the seed scripts are not in the image. They are: the API image copies `scripts/` and
   `packages/`. What keeps real data out of a shipped build is the data side, unchanged: the corpus is
   never in the repository or an image, the packaging gate refuses anything under
   `OspreyFlow_Data/Enron_Mails`, and the seed refuses without the exceptions entry.
2. The data folder is `OspreyFlow_Data/Enron_Mails/` (ADR-053 and ADR-054 say `enron/`).
3. The exceptions list is a gitignored file on the host, which the container cannot see. The host
   command (`scripts/seed_internal.py`) checks `is_permitted("enron", "owner_run_demonstration")`
   before starting anything and tells the seed with `--attested-permission`; run directly on the host
   the seed checks it itself. Both refuse, with a sentence, when the entry is missing.

**Built, tests first:** the Enron reader and its seed (now `internal_demos/enron.py` and
`internal_demos/seed_enron.py`, ADR-114 Amendment 2), the `enron` registry manifest
(`internal`), `make seed-enron`. The case is "Enron corpus (real data, this machine only)", with no
unit-wide level, the demo admin as Author and the demo analyst as Editor (ADR-053 point 5).
**Not yet run** against the real corpus or a real ArcadeDB from here.

### ADR-052, Amendment 10 (30 September 2026) — the synthetic demos join the same route

`hmp` and `fixture-corp` now load through `scripts/seed_internal.py` (`make seed-hmp`,
`make seed-fixture-corp`) into named cases, "HMP fixture (synthetic demo)" and "Fixture Corp
(synthetic demo)", shared with the demo admin (Author) and analyst (Editor). Their seeds take
`--case-name` and `--grant` beside the existing `--investigation-scope`, which still works, so
`harness.apply --seed` is unchanged. They generate their own data, so no data folder is mounted and no
attestation is passed.

### ADR-055, Amendment 3 (30 September 2026) — an interrupted seed can be resumed; progress is shown

**Seen.** The owner's first `make seed-paysim` ran for over five hours with a single line of output (the
case name) and was stopped with Ctrl-C. Nothing could tell slow from stuck. The graph write is one
lookup and one write per element over HTTP, so hours is plausible on a laptop, and it was silent. I
had also told the owner it "should take minutes" without ever having run it on a real ArcadeDB: that
was a guess and is withdrawn. A plain re-run would then have refused ("already loaded") on the
half-written graph, and had it not, would have doubled the events (the analytics load is an INSERT).

**Built, tests first (`scripts/seed_support.py`, used by the PaySim and Enron seeds):**

1. The graph write prints a line every 25 batches with the elapsed time, so a slow write is visible as
   slow and the rate can be read off after a minute. The host command shows the seed's output as it
   arrives instead of at the end.
2. `--resume` (`make`'s `seed_internal ... --resume`) skips the "graph already loaded" refusal. Safe
   because the graph write is an upsert keyed on id; nothing is deleted.
3. A seed refuses, before the graph phase, to load events into a case that already has any, so a
   resume can never double the counts and the owner is never made to wait hours to be refused.

**Not decided here:** how fast the graph write can be made. Bulk writing would bypass the adapter's
per-element lookups and is a design change to the adapter; I will only propose it once a real run has
shown the rate.

### ADR-055, Amendment 4 (30 September 2026) — replace, not resume; the graph is a sample

**Seen, on the owner's machine.** With progress lines on, the graph write's rate was visible: about 65 ms
per account (74,000 accounts took 80 minutes) and 340 ms per transaction, *rising* to 470 ms by the
eighth thousand as the graph grew. The adapter runs several lookups per transaction, one of them a
total over every transaction of that type already stored, so the cost grows with the graph. The
projection for the remaining 57,000 transactions was many hours. The owner stopped the run.

**Amendment 3 is corrected on one point.** It says `--resume` was safe because the graph write is an
upsert. That holds for accounts and is **false for transactions**: writing a transaction that already
exists adds to its occurrence count (`upsert_edges` merges occurrences), which inflates weights.
`--resume` is withdrawn and removed. The progress lines and the refusal to load events twice stand.

**Decided with the owner's agreement ("I agree with your recommended approach"):**

1. **`--replace-graph` replaces `--resume`.** It deletes this seed's own graph rows and only those
   (every statement is scoped by the seed's id prefix, `paysim-acct-`/`paysim-tx-` or
   `enron-ep-`/`enron-comm-`, because the account and edge types are shared between datasets),
   transactions first, and raises if any are left, then loads fresh.
2. **The PaySim graph is a sample.** The first 500 fraud transactions in file order and everything
   touching their accounts: roughly 5,000 accounts and 4,000 transactions, about half an hour. The
   analytics store still gets every row, so counts, time windows and amounts cover all 6.36 million.
   `--graph-fraud-rows N` changes the size; `all` restores the full neighbourhood. This narrows
   ADR-055's point 1 for the graph only (its "fraud neighbourhood" is now the sampled neighbourhood
   by default); the analytics side is unchanged.

**Not decided, and not built:** a fast bulk-write mode in the graph adapter (skipping the per-element
lookups on a fresh load) would load the full graph in minutes. It changes the adapter's behaviour and
cannot be tested here (no ArcadeDB in the build environment), so it waits for the owner to see the
sample and ask for it.

**Untested against a real ArcadeDB:** the two delete statements (`DELETE EDGE` and `DELETE VERTEX` with
a `LIKE` on the id prefix) are proved only against a fake that answers the statements the code
sends. The clean-up prints how many rows it removed and fails if any remain, so a statement the
database rejects or ignores is visible on the first run.

### ADR-055, Amendment 5 (30 September 2026) — ArcadeDB's delete syntax was not the one I wrote

**Seen, on the owner's machine.** `--replace-graph` stopped at its first delete: ArcadeDB's SQL parser
refused `DELETE EDGE <type> WHERE ...` (a `ParseException`). Amendment 4 had said the delete statements
were untested against a real ArcadeDB; this is what that risk looked like. Nothing was written or
deleted, because the failure came before the load, but the owner lost a run and the Conduit was
restarted.

**Fix.** The clean-up tries the documented forms in turn: `DELETE FROM <type> WHERE id LIKE '<prefix>%'`,
then `DELETE EDGE|VERTEX <type> WHERE ...`, then the Gremlin bridge the adapter already uses
(`g.E()|g.V().hasLabel(...).has('id', TextP.startingWith(...)).drop()`). Only a *parse* refusal moves
on to the next form; any other error is raised as it is. Every form is scoped by the label and the id
prefix, transactions go before accounts, and the count afterwards must be zero. If no form is accepted
the error lists every one tried and nothing has been deleted. Which form ArcadeDB accepts is still
unproven from here: the first run on the owner's machine will show it.

### ADR-055, Amendment 6 (30 September 2026) — a read-only inspection, after the second failed clean-up

**Seen, on the owner's machine.** With the delete forms of Amendment 5, ArcadeDB accepted
`DELETE FROM <edge type> WHERE id LIKE 'paysim-tx-%'` (so that syntax is right) and then failed with a
404, `RecordNotFoundException`, for record `#169:80`. Nothing had been deleted. A record that a
delete reaches but the database cannot find is an inconsistency, most likely left by the two loads
that were interrupted mid-write (an index entry, or an edge list on a vertex, pointing at a record
that is not there). I do not know which, and I will not guess a third time against the owner's
database or reach for something drastic such as dropping it.

**Built:** `--inspect` (and `--inspect-record <id>`), a mode that sends only `SELECT` statements, needs no
case and no demo accounts, leaves the Conduit running, and reports each probe on its own so a failing
one is shown as the evidence and the rest still run: counts of all vertices and edges, of the account
and transaction types with and without the seed's id prefix, three transaction ids, and the named
record. `python -m scripts.seed_internal paysim --inspect --inspect-record '#169:80'`. The fix
to the clean-up will follow from what it shows.

### ADR-055, Amendment 7 (30 September 2026) — when a row delete cannot find a record, empty the types, guarded

**Seen (Amendment 6's inspection, owner's machine).** Every row in the account type (73,863) and in the
transaction type (9,205) carries this seed's id prefix, so nothing else lives in those two types.
Record `#169:80` exists and reads normally (a `TRANSACTED` edge, revision 2, written by the first
load and updated by the resumed one). The 404 is therefore not a lost record; the likely cause is a
dangling link in an account's edge list left by the interrupted loads. This is a diagnosis by
inference, not proven. The inspection's "all vertices"/"all edges" probes failed because this
ArcadeDB has no generic `V`/`E` types; they are removed. It also ended with "paysim is loaded",
which was false; it now says nothing was changed.

**Decided (owner agreed to clearing and rebuilding).** When the row-by-row delete fails with a
missing-record error, `clear_seeded_graph` falls back to `TRUNCATE TYPE <type> UNSAFE`, edge type
first, then the account type. The types are shared with other datasets, so the fallback runs only if
*every* row in each type carries this seed's prefix (counted with and without the prefix); if either
type holds anything else it truncates nothing and raises. The count afterwards must still be zero.
The normal path never truncates. The whole database is not dropped: truncating the two types reaches
the same clean graph faster and touches nothing else.

### ADR-055, Amendment 8 (30 September 2026) — a truncate the client gives up on is waited for, and the clean-up says what it is doing

**Seen, on the owner's machine.** The Amendment 7 fallback worked as designed: the row delete met the
missing record, the guard passed, and `TRUNCATE TYPE ... UNSAFE` was sent. The adapter's HTTP client
then gave up after its 30-second timeout (`httpx.ReadTimeout`) and the seed aborted. Emptying ~74,000
rows takes longer than that, and the server does not stop when the client does, so the graph was left
in a state the seed could not describe. The clean-up had also printed nothing, which is what made the
earlier run look hung.

**Decided.** A client timeout on the truncate is not a failure. The seed waits, counting the rows left
in that type every 10 seconds (a count that itself times out is retried), until it is empty or 30
minutes have passed, and raises, naming the type and pointing at `--inspect`, if it is not. The
adapter's timeout is unchanged: no image rebuild is needed. `clear_seeded_graph` now prints what it is
doing (the counts to remove, the fallback, each type emptying and how many rows are left).

### ADR-055, Amendment 9 (30 September 2026) — an explicit `--reset-graph-database`, after the storage itself proved damaged

**Seen, on the owner's machine.** With the truncate and its wait (Amendments 7 and 8) the graph
loaded 13,564 accounts and about 2,400 transactions, then ArcadeDB answered the adapter's
occurrence-sum lookup with a 500, `java.nio.BufferUnderflowException`. The read-only inspection then
showed 2,400 rows in the transaction type of which 2,399 carry this seed's id prefix, so one stored
row is unlike the rest. ArcadeDB's own log records, as SEVERE, `Error on loading record #169:80
(Error on fetching multi page record #169:80)`. The 13,564 accounts contradict a size limit (the
resumed run reached more than 8,000 transactions). This is a diagnosis by inference, not proof: the
storage holds at least one record ArcadeDB cannot read back, most likely from the interrupted loads
and the forced truncate; the `BufferUnderflowException` itself is not in the log tail.

**Decided (owner: "delete the databases and rebuild from the beginning").** Row-level clean-up cannot
repair unreadable storage, so `seed_paysim` gains `--reset-graph-database` (passed through by
`seed_internal`, PaySim only for now, and never on by default). It drops the whole graph database,
waits out a client timeout on the drop as Amendment 8 does for the truncate, checks it is gone,
creates it empty, and the seed then applies the schema and loads as usual. Everything in that
database goes, every case's graph rows, which is why the seed says so before doing it and why the
option must be asked for. The Conduit is stopped for the run as before. Analytics events and case
records are elsewhere and are not touched. The seed already creates the database and applies the
schema, so nothing else needs doing before the load.

## ADR-056 — A vault per dataset: separate stores for each dataset, one control plane, and a read-only shared vault

**Status: Accepted in principle, 30 September 2026 (owner's rulings recorded below). Nothing is built.
Delivery is staged (section 6); each stage lands green before the next starts.**

### Context: what was seen

Loading PaySim on the owner's machine (ADR-055) showed what one graph database for every dataset costs.
As the code stands, the Conduit opens one ArcadeDB database, `ospreyflow` (hard-coded in
`services/api/app.py` and `worker_main.py`; 14 places construct an ArcadeDB client outside the tests), and
every seed writes into it, separated only by id prefix (`paysim-acct-`, `enron-ep-`), `owning_unit` and
case access on the events side. Four costs were seen or follow directly:

- **Blast radius.** A damaged load needed the whole graph database dropped (ADR-055 Amendment 9), which
  would have taken every other dataset with it.
- **Cross-contaminated weights.** The adapter weighs each edge from corpus-wide degrees and totals
  (`corpus_total_occurrences`, `corpus_source_degree`), so loading one dataset changes the weights of
  another's edges.
- **Write cost grows with everything.** Every edge write scans all edges of its type.
- **Real data is hard to remove or exclude.** ADR-053 keeps Enron on the owner's machine; a database that
  can be dropped, backed up or left out of a package by name is a cleaner boundary than deleting rows by
  prefix.

`00_ARCHITECTURE.md` (Non-goals) says: "No multi-tenancy in v1. One deployment serves one organisation.
Handling markings partition data within it; they are not a tenancy boundary." The owner's answer:
analysts in the same organisation work on different datasets as a normal case, and segregation gives each
dataset a **sterile corridor**. That is not tenancy, and this record says so.

### Decisions (the owner's rulings)

1. **Words.** "The Vault" stays the name of the whole backend tier (`00_ARCHITECTURE.md`,
   `04_VAULT_BACKEND.md`). **A vault** is one dataset's isolated set of stores inside it. **The shared
   vault** ("the OspreyFlow Vault") is the common one. A vault is not a tenant: one deployment, one
   organisation, several vaults. **This amends the non-goal quoted above**; that line is not edited, and
   carries a pointer to this record.
2. **The unit is the dataset.** A vault equals a dataset; a case belongs to exactly one vault; many
   cases may share a vault (two analysts on PaySim have two cases in one vault). Choosing a dataset at the
   start of a session in the Glass or Ingest Studio chooses the active vault for that session.
3. **What is per vault.** The graph database; the analytics (DuckDB) file; the working-set cache
   namespace; the object-store bucket; the search and embeddings index. **Models are shared**, not
   duplicated; what is per vault is which models the vault may use (a real-data vault may forbid external
   ones), its prompts and settings, its analysis history and its embeddings.
4. **The Conduit is not segregated.** One vault-aware Conduit remains the control plane: Keycloak identity,
   cases and access (ADR-052), audit, and job orchestration stay central, because the case picker must
   list across vaults. Every request and every job carries a vault id, and the ports are built **per
   vault with no default**, so a missing vault id fails instead of reaching another dataset's database.
   A process-isolated Conduit for a real-data vault is possible later; it is not built now.
5. **Sterile corridor.** The only flow across a vault boundary is **from the shared vault into a vault,
   read-only, and every such read is audited**. No vault reads another vault. Cross-dataset linking, if it
   is ever wanted, needs its own design; it does not come free from sharing a database.
6. **The shared vault.** First release: the ontology, recipes, patterns and provider profiles, as
   versioned content that a vault **pins** to (a live reference would let one change alter another vault's
   results, which is the weighting problem again). **Read-only for everyone except vault administrators**,
   who set it up. **A new `vault-admin` role** (a Keycloak role distinct from a case's Author), so owning a
   case never implies write access to shared content. Reusable algorithms are added later as their own
   decision.
7. **Naming (default, accepted).** Vault ids are short and stable (`paysim`, `enron`, `hmp`,
   `fixture-corp`); physical names derive from them (`vault_<id>` for the graph database, a per-vault
   directory for the DuckDB file). To be confirmed when the registry is built.

### The existing PaySim load, and the other seeds

Nothing done so far removes the PaySim already in `ospreyflow`, and `--reset-graph-database` is not to be
run against it again. **Stage 0:** re-seed PaySim into a new, named vault (the seeds already read
`ARCADEDB_DATABASE`; `seed_internal` does not pass it yet, which is a small change), about 40 minutes and
deterministic. The original stays live until the owner retires it, because the Glass reads `ospreyflow`
until routing exists. **Enron is held** until its own vault exists; HMP and Fixture Corp are reloaded into
their own vaults later.

### Consequences, and what is not yet known

- **Work.** My estimate is three to five weeks: ADR and spec (about 1 day); a vault registry and resolver
  replacing the hard-coded names (3 to 5 days); binding a case to a vault, and choosing the vault in the
  Glass and Ingest Studio, with cache and working-set scoping (4 to 6 days); create, reset and back up per
  vault, and seeds that take `--vault` (3 to 4 days); the shared vault and pinning (4 to 6 days);
  acceptance rows, leakage tests and the full suite on the owner's Mac (3 to 5 days).
- **Unsized.** The Glass changes, and how many Conduit routes assume one global graph (about 50 places
  refer to a case or scope), are the largest unknowns. The estimate gets revised at the end of stage 1.
- **First slice (stage 1):** a graph database and a DuckDB file per vault behind a fixed registry, proved
  with PaySim; cache, index, object store and model scoping follow.
- **The main risk** is a code path that reaches a vault without a vault id; the tests must prove that is
  impossible, and leakage between two vaults gets acceptance rows of its own.
- **What this does not decide:** cross-vault linking; how a vault is retired or archived; whether the
  shared vault is mirrored into each vault for offline use.

### ADR-056, Amendment 1 (30 September 2026) — stage 0: the PaySim seed takes a vault, and the shared stores are cleared afterwards

**Owner's ruling.** After the new PaySim vault is verified, **drop the `ospreyflow` graph database and
the analytics events and create them clean** (case records stay). Not before: until stage 1 (routing)
the Glass reads only the shared stores, so dropping first would leave no fallback if the re-seed failed.

**Built (stage 0a).** `seed_paysim` and `seed_internal` take `--vault <id>`. The vault's graph database is
`vault_<id>` (hyphens become underscores) and its analytics file is
`<the deployment's analytics directory>/vaults/<id>/analytics.duckdb`, both derived from the id inside
the container, so the graph and the events always move together. An id is lower-case letters, digits and
