**Not decided here, and not built.** ForceAtlas2 in a worker for the 50,000-node and 250,000-edge case (02_GLASS_FRONTEND.md
section 5), which is still unmeasured. Dragging a node by hand, and so a pin that survives a re-layout (the layout supports
a pinned node; nothing in the canvas pins one yet). A visual check in a real browser: the tests cover the layout's behaviour
(spreading, attraction, repeatability, a pinned node, the size cap), not whether it looks right.

### Amendment 1 (3 October 2026) — an expansion that would add more than 500 nodes asks first

**Seen.** A double-click on a busy Enron address added all 1,090 of its neighbours at once (1,091 nodes, 1,163 edges). That is
past the layout's own limit of 1,000, so no layout ran and the result was an unreadable disc. The double-click had been built
without the count-first check the owner had agreed.

**Decision.** Every way of expanding a node (double-click, a right-click menu entry, the Enter key) goes through one function
that first asks `/expand/preview` how many nodes it would add. Up to 500 it goes ahead. Above 500, or when the count could not be
obtained, nothing is added until the analyst chooses: a single relationship type (each shown with its own count), everything, or
nothing. The limit is `EXPANSION_CONFIRM_ABOVE` in `canvas/expansionGate.ts`.

**Not built.** "Add the strongest 100": the expand request has no limit field, so it needs a server change. Whether 500 is the
right number has not been tried on a real screen.


## ADR-061 — Type-ahead search takes options: match mode, ignore case, entity types

Status: accepted 3 October 2026.

Context. ADR-059 gave the Glass a type-ahead box that matched the start of a value, case-sensitively, across every entity type. The owner asked for filters: ignore case, entity type, match mode (starts with, contains, exact) and a scope limited to the graph on screen.

Decision.

1. `/v1/suggest` gains three optional fields: `mode` (`starts_with` default, `contains`, `exact`), `ignore_case` (false default) and `types` (list of entity types, at most 50). Defaults reproduce ADR-059 exactly.
2. The port takes a frozen `SuggestOptions`. An unknown entity type is a `ValueError` in the adapter and a 422 at the route; it is never silently dropped.
3. Case-sensitive forms use the predicates already proven on the store (`TextP.startingWith`, `TextP.containing`, `P.eq`).
4. Ignoring case uses `TextP.regex` with a `(?iu)` flag and the typed text quoted as a literal (`\Q...\E`), so characters such as `.`, `*` and `(` are text. This is unproven on ArcadeDB. Four live conformance cases (ignoring case, contains and exact, typed regex characters are text, access filtering with ignore case) were written first and must be run against a live store before this is relied on.
5. Contains and ignore-case cannot use an index. Their cost on the Enron data is unmeasured; ADR-059's 300 ms threshold applies once measured.
6. Searching only the graph on screen is client-side over the drawn nodes and does not call this endpoint.
7. The Filters panel in the Glass is not built by this decision; it follows as its own step.

Consequences. The audit record of a suggestion includes mode, ignore_case and types. Access filtering is unchanged and runs after matching.


## ADR-062 — The view can be tidied: remove selected nodes, or clear the view

Status: accepted 3 October 2026.

Context. After a large expansion the owner could not clear the graph and had no way to drop nodes they did not want ("I cannot clear out the graph once it is rendered").

Decision.

1. A **Remove selected (n)** button and the Delete or Backspace key take the selected nodes out of the working set. **Clear view** removes every node, after a confirmation that names the count and says the records stay in the store and History can restore them.
2. Both use the existing `DELETE /v1/investigations/{id}/nodes` route. No new endpoint. The server records a History step and publishes a remove delta.
3. The graph changes only after the server confirms (a reply with a sequence number). A refusal or a failed request shows the error and leaves every node where it was.
4. Removal is from the view only. No record, edge or assertion is deleted from the store.

Consequences. Delete and Backspace now act on the canvas when something is selected; they do nothing when nothing is selected. Removing an edge on its own comes with selectable links, not here.


### ADR-061 Amendment 1 — The Filters panel is built (3 October 2026)

Item 7 of ADR-061 said the Glass panel was not yet built. It now is: a **Filters** button under the search box opens a panel with an ignore-case tick box, the match mode (starts with, contains, exact), the entity types from the ontology (none ticked means every type) and "Only nodes on screen". The button shows how many filters are on. Changing a filter asks the question again.

With every filter at its default the request is exactly the one ADR-059 defined; a changed filter is sent under the Conduit's own names, and an unchanged one is left out. "Only nodes on screen" asks the Conduit nothing: it compares the typed text with the identifiers of the nodes drawn, as plain text (never a pattern), honouring ignore case, match mode and type, and it searches from the first character. It matches the same identifier properties the box already shows, which is not necessarily every field the Conduit searches.

Still unproven: ignoring case against the real store (the four live conformance cases from ADR-061 have not been run).


## ADR-063 — The analyst chooses how the working set is arranged

Status: accepted 3 October 2026.

Context. The owner found the graph unreadable after a large expansion ("no way to reformat the layout"), and a second review asked for several layout algorithms: organic by default, hierarchical, and grouping.

Decision.

1. A **Layout** menu on the canvas offers five arrangements: Organic (the force layout of ADR-060, the default), Radial around the selected node, Hierarchical, Circular and Group by type. Choosing one arranges at once and applies to nodes added afterwards until another is chosen. **Arrange again** repeats the current one, which re-centres a radial layout on whatever is now selected.
2. The four new layouts are pure functions in `canvas/layoutModes.ts`, behind one `arrange(mode, input, options)` interface. Positions are repeatable for the same graph. Above 6,000 nodes none is attempted and the positions stay.
3. **Hierarchical is our own small implementation**: edges that close a cycle are set aside, each node goes on the layer below its deepest parent, and four barycentre sweeps reorder each layer to reduce crossings. It is not a full Sugiyama layout (no optimal crossing minimisation, no dummy nodes for long edges). It sits behind `arrange`, so dagre or another library can replace it later without touching the canvas. No library was downloaded.
4. Radial uses the first selected node as the centre, or the most connected node when nothing is selected. Choosing a different node does not re-arrange by itself, so clicking around does not move the graph under the analyst's hands.
5. Nothing is stored: a layout is a view of positions, never a change to the data.

Not decided here. Communities (collapsing a group into one node) is a separate step.

Consequences. The layout choice is per session in the browser tab and is not remembered. Radial, hierarchical and circular ignore pinned nodes, which the force layout supports.


## ADR-064 — A link can be selected, and shown in the Inspector

Status: accepted 3 October 2026.

Context. The owner could not select links ("I am not able to select the links themselves"). A link was only inspectable through a popup that opened on hover, anchored at the pointer, so the click that followed landed on the popup. The drawn line is also one or two pixels wide, and the renderer picks a link only where it is drawn.

Decision.

1. A click on a link selects it: it is drawn thicker, in brass, with its label, and the Inspector shows its type, the direction between its two ends (or that it has none), how many records stand behind it, its dates, its provenance and its sources. Selecting a link clears the node selection and the other way round, so the Inspector shows one thing.
2. The click target is wider than the line. A click that the renderer did not attribute to a node or a link is checked against every visible link in screen space, with a reach of 6 pixels, before it counts as a click on empty space. The arithmetic is a pure function (`canvas/edgeSelection.ts`); a browser test proves a click 4 pixels off selects, one 16 pixels off does not.
3. Hovering a link opens nothing. The hover popup is removed; its component is left unused.
4. Keyboard (rule 13): with a node focused, `L` selects its next link and `Shift+L` the previous, wrapping round.
5. Delete (or Backspace) on a selected link, and a **Hide selected link** button, hide it from the view **in this browser tab only**. A **Show hidden links (n)** button brings them back, and a reload resets it. This is not recorded in History and nothing is sent to the server, because the server has no way to remove one link from the working set today. Hiding a link on the server, undoable through History, would need a new route and delta; it was offered and not chosen.

Not decided here. Deleting a link from the store; selecting several links.

Consequences. A hidden link still counts in the working set and in layout. The details panel for a link reads only what the working set already holds.


## ADR-065 — The top bar: menus for case and account, an application switch, Filters inside the search box

Status: accepted 3 October 2026.

Context. The owner looked at the Glass at about 1,000 pixels wide and found the top bar cluttered ("I don't think we need the case selector expanded here"): the case choice was a bare white box with `All cases` and `New case` stacked under it, `Filters` dropped below the search box looking like a stray button, and `Export`, `Sign out` and the long user id broke over two lines. Two causes were in the stylesheet, not the layout: `.select { composes: input; }` is CSS-modules syntax and does nothing in a plain stylesheet, so every `<Select>` was drawn with the browser's own white face (the same white boxes appear on the Ingest Studio's Connector and Handling marking choices); and the search box's Filters button and the header's buttons had no rules at all. The owner then asked for the Ingest Studio to stand apart from the Glass ("I want to distinguish clearly between the apps") and chose, from three offered designs, the application switch below.

Decision.

1. A shared dropdown panel (`design/primitives/DropdownPanel.tsx`): a button that opens a panel beneath it. Closes on Escape (focus returns to the button), on a click outside, and when keyboard focus moves outside it.
2. The case choice becomes `Case: <name> ▾`, opening the list of cases (the open one marked), `All cases` and `New case`. The Ingest Studio's "goes into" row uses the same component.
3. The account becomes one button, `<user name> · <clearance> ▾`, at the right-hand end. The user name may be cut short; the clearance is never cut short, so ADR-050's "always visible" holds. The panel shows the subject, clearance, unit and `Sign out`. `DisplayPrincipal` gains `username` from the token's `preferred_username` (empty when absent; the subject is shown instead).
4. Filters is an icon inside the search box at its right-hand end, with a small count when filters are on. Its accessible name is unchanged (`Filters`, `Filters (n)`).
5. An application switch at the far left, `[Glass | Ingest Studio]`, the open one filled in brass; while the Ingest Studio is open, a brass line under the bar and the Glass-only controls are not shown. Choosing Glass returns to the Glass view last open.
6. `.select` is given the input's own rules. Whole items of the bar wrap to a second line in a narrow window; labels never break.

Not decided here. A different accent colour per application (offered, not chosen). Removing the Ingest Studio's own case row now that the bar carries the case menu in both applications (both are kept).

Consequences. The bar is one line from about 1,440 pixels wide (measured in a browser with a stand-in for the slider's width); narrower windows wrap. The case name in the button is cut at 200 pixels. Existing tests were changed where the controls moved (the case switcher tests now open the menu first; the Ingest tab test names the button `Ingest Studio`). `App.test.tsx`'s fixture was also corrected: its handling-scheme stub had the wrong shape and its other answers did not suit the screens the new tests reach, so the new tests hold every request unanswered. Not exercised: the real `App` bar in a browser (the browser tests render the same components in a harness, `keyboard/top-bar-harness.tsx`); the light theme.


## ADR-067 — Upload from the analyst's computer into the ingest folder (amends ruling R6)

Status: accepted 3 October 2026.

Context. Ruling R6 (27 September 2026) gave Connect a list of the files in a read-only ingest folder and deferred any browser upload past the milestone. The owner opened the Ingest Studio and said: "I need a file picker, not just the bar saying file path." With an empty folder the screen offered only a text box, and a path typed from an analyst's own machine names nothing the Conduit's container can open. The owner chose "Upload from my computer".

Decision.

1. `POST /v1/ingest/source-files?name=<file name>` takes the file's bytes as the raw request body and writes them to `<ingest root>/uploaded/<name>`. `SOURCE_AUTHOR` only, checked before any byte is read. It returns the same shape as a listing entry, marked `uploaded`.
2. It refuses, with a sentence the Glass shows as given: a name with a folder part, a leading dot, a control character or over 200 characters (400); an extension outside the connectors' list (415); a name already used in the root or in `uploaded`, so nothing is ever overwritten (409); an empty file (400); a file over `OSPREY_INGEST_MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES`, default 512 MiB (413). The size is counted as the body streams and the declared length is checked first.
3. The bytes go to a hidden part-file and are linked into place only when complete; a refused or interrupted upload leaves nothing behind and a half-written file is never listed.
4. The audit record holds the name and the size, never the contents.
5. The renderer keeps the root's mount read-only (R6 is unchanged for operator-placed evidence) and lays one writable bind mount over its `uploaded/` sub-folder (`INGEST_UPLOAD_SUBDIR`, tested equal to the Conduit's own `UPLOAD_SUBDIR`).
6. The listing now includes the `uploaded/` folder (files only; a symlink or folder inside it is not offered; the same resolve-then-compare check applies), each entry carrying `uploaded: true|false`.
7. Connect shows **Choose file…** first (a real button that presses a hidden file input, so the keyboard reaches it), then the list of what is already on the server, and the typed path behind "Or type a path or address". The chosen file is selected as the data as soon as it has uploaded.

Not decided here. Deleting an uploaded file (nothing removes one yet); a quota across all uploads; scanning an upload for malware; uploading to a deployment whose ingest folder is on object storage.

Consequences. The Conduit can now write inside the ingest root, but only inside `uploaded/`. The write path is covered by module and route tests (names, no overwrite, size limit stopping the read, no leftovers, role, audit) and the mount by two renderer tests. **None of it has been run against Docker by the session that wrote it.** The known risk is Linux host ownership: Docker creates a missing host folder as root, and the Conduit runs as uid 10001, so the operator must create `uploaded/` and give that uid write access (`05_DEPLOYMENT.md`); Docker Desktop on macOS maps ownership itself. If the folder is not writable, the upload fails with a server error rather than a sentence, which is the first thing to check if the owner's first upload fails.


## ADR-068 — A blank classification on Connect is recorded as PUBLIC

Status: accepted 3 October 2026.

Context. Spec 09 §2 said none of Connect's three answers is optional. The owner looked at the Connect form and said the classification "needs to include public and also it does not need to be mandatory", and ruled "Blank means PUBLIC" when offered a scheme-named default instead (my recommendation was a default named in the scheme; the owner chose differently).

Decision.

1. The UK scheme (`packages/ontology/handling/uk-le.yaml`) gains `PUBLIC` as its lowest level: `[PUBLIC, OFFICIAL, OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE, SECRET]`. Dominance is by position, so every existing marking keeps its rank relative to the others, an `OFFICIAL` reader clears `PUBLIC`, and a `PUBLIC` reader does not clear `OFFICIAL`.
2. When a draft is created or edited with no classification (missing, empty or blank), the server records the scheme's lowest level, `PUBLIC` when the scheme has it and otherwise its first level. The Glass does not decide this; it only says "Left blank: recorded as PUBLIC" beside the box.
3. An analyst's own choice is never replaced. The other parts of the handling marking (handling code, originator, owning unit) and the legal basis stay required for Profile.
4. Spec 09 §2 is amended to say so.

Not decided here. Whether a blank classification should warn when the source was supplied by another unit; adding a `PUBLIC` level to the US scheme (it has its own lowest level, `UNCLASSIFIED`, which a blank marking takes there).

Consequences. A blank marking is the least protective marking, so a source loaded without thought is visible to every principal who clears `PUBLIC`. That is the owner's ruling and is why the screen says so rather than hiding it. Nothing in storage changes shape; a `PUBLIC` value is an ordinary classification string. Demo realm clearances (`harness/realm.py`) and every existing seed are unaffected because none carries `PUBLIC` as a clearance.


## ADR-066 — Communities on screen: boxes round groups of closely linked nodes, folded into one Group Node (appended after ADR-068; numbered earlier because the code cites it)

Status: accepted 3 October 2026.

Context. A busy view is a tangle: the owner asked for the nodes that belong together to be shown as groups the analyst can fold away and open again ("Communities"). Nothing in the spec described grouping on screen; ADR-029's Louvain (with a connected-components fix) runs in the compute tiers for the Metrics panel; the canvas does its own, lighter grouping of just the nodes in view.

Decision.

1. A `Communities` button on the canvas (reached by Tab, pressed by Enter or Space) switches the view on and off. When on, the nodes now in the view are divided into groups by Louvain with a fixed seed, so the same nodes fall into the same groups each time. A node with no link to another is in no group. Nothing is stored and nothing is sent to the server: it is a way of looking at the view, and switching it off puts everything back.
2. Each group is drawn as a box round its nodes, kept a fixed 16 pixels clear of them whatever the zoom. A box has a fold button (labelled `Fold group of N nodes`).
3. Folding turns a group into one Group Node: the group's best-connected member is drawn larger with a brass ring and labelled with what the group holds; the other members are drawn at the same place, too small to see, so a link from outside the group still reaches the Group Node, and links inside the group are not drawn. Opening it puts every member back where it was.
4. Ways to fold and open, all reachable by keyboard: the box's button; `G` on a focused node (folds its group, or opens it when it is the Group Node); `Collapse all` and `Expand all` beside the Communities button; a double-click inside a box folds it; a double-click on a Group Node opens it (and does not ask the server to expand anything).
5. While a group is folded: keyboard walking, ring walking and the lasso skip the members that are not drawn; a selected or focused hidden member is moved to the Group Node; Delete on a lone Group Node opens it rather than removing it, unless the whole group is being removed; the status bar says how many nodes are folded into groups (spec 02 §2: the bar never lies).

How a folded group is drawn. Sigma reads every node's position from the graph on each draw and ignores a position returned by a reducer (confirmed in `sigma.cjs.dev.js`, `process()`, and in a real browser, where the Group Node was drawn at the stand-in's own place). So the folded members' stored positions are really moved to the group's centre and their true positions kept aside; a position written afterwards (a layout, a drag) is noticed because it no longer matches where the member was put, and becomes its true position. Opening, switching Communities off, or a member leaving the group puts the true position back. The force layout starts from the true positions.

Not decided here. Naming a group by something other than its size; remembering which groups are folded between sessions; grouping by a property (the Layout menu's group-by-type does that for position only).

Consequences. While a group is folded the working set's stored x and y for its members are the group's centre, so anything that reads them directly sees the centre (the Metrics hulls do, which is right for a folded group). Not tested in a browser: a layout run while a group is folded (the logic above handles it, no test drives it). The on-screen Louvain does not apply ADR-029's connected-components split, so a group can in principle be made of two pieces that are not linked to each other. Louvain on a very large view is done on the main thread each time the working set changes; unmeasured, and the performance gate in spec 02 section 5 does not cover it.


## ADR-069 — Declutter, first part: the timeline's rarely used boxes behind buttons, and a quieter drawing for a crowded view

Status: accepted 3 October 2026.

Context. The owner found the workspace cluttered. Two causes are fixed here; the rest of the declutter list (the Metrics panel, the judgement badges, a light and dark theme, drawing three degrees out on a search selection) is not decided and is not built.

Decision.

1. The timeline's two boxes for typing exact dates (`from (ISO)`, `to (ISO)`) are behind a `Set exact dates` button in the timeline's own bar, closed until pressed (`aria-expanded` says which). Spec 02 section 3.4's "Brush endpoints are editable as text" still holds; the text boxes are one press away.
2. The `Overlay investigation` row above the timeline, a labelled box that was always showing, becomes an `Overlay another case` button in the timeline's own bar that reveals the same box (accessible name unchanged: `Cross-case overlay investigation id`). While a second investigation is overlaid, the button names it. The row above the timeline is gone, so the chart has that height back.
3. A crowded view is drawn quieter. Node size is multiplied, and link width multiplied, by a scale that is 1 up to 150 nodes (or links) and falls steadily on a log scale to 0.55 at 3,000 and beyond. A node is never drawn smaller than 2, nor a link thinner than 0.5, and a link on a found path keeps its width. The scale depends only on how many there are: nothing is hidden, so spec 02 section 1.1's "zoom never changes what exists" and the status bar's counts are unaffected.

Not decided here. The 150, 3,000 and 0.55 are first guesses to be tuned by looking at a real busy view; they are named constants in `canvas/nodeAttributes.ts`.

Consequences. The live scenario B specs press the two new buttons first (changed, not run: they need the owner's seeded stack). A drawing change cannot be judged by a unit test, so what is tested is the arithmetic (it shrinks, has a floor, leaves a small view and a found path alone) and not how it looks; the owner should look at a few hundred nodes and say whether it is quieter enough.


## ADR-070 — Declutter, second part: Metrics in closed sections, a count on nodes that have judgements, three steps drawn on a search selection, and a light and dark choice

Status: accepted 3 October 2026 (the four choices were put to the owner and each recommended option was taken).

Context. ADR-069 left four items of the owner's declutter list undecided. They were put to the owner as four questions and answered; this records the answers and what was built.

Decision.

1. **Metrics panel.** It opens closed. Inside it there are two sections, `Ranking` and `Communities`, and only one is open at a time (each heading is a button with `aria-expanded`). Neither metric is fetched until its section is opened, so a closed panel costs the server nothing. Spec 02 section 3.2's "ranked list, not a chart", "clicking a row selects and centres that node" and the hull overlay are unchanged.
2. **Judgement badges.** A node that has at least one judgement resting on it (listed as supporting or contradicting) carries a small brass count beside it on the canvas, labelled `N judgement(s)` for a screen reader. It shows that a judgement exists and nothing about the judgement: no probability band, no text. It is drawn only from the judgements the signed-in principal can already list, through the existing judgements route, so it opens no new read path and cannot reveal a judgement the principal may not see (`CLAUDE.md` rules 3 and 4; spec 02 section 9.2's hidden-judgement rule is therefore unchanged). The badge ignores the pointer, so it never gets in the way of a click or a drag.
3. **Choosing a search result.** The node is put on the canvas and drawn out three links (`SEARCH_DRAW_DEPTH = 3`) in one request, not one link as before. The server counts the result first, and above the existing 500-node gate the canvas asks before drawing and keeps the three steps in the answer; nothing is cut silently (`CLAUDE.md` rule 2). The expand request already carried a depth (1 to 4), so no server change was needed.
4. **Light and dark.** A button in the top bar (`Light theme`, `aria-pressed`) switches between the two themes already defined in `tokens.css`. The choice is kept in this browser only (`localStorage`, key `ospreyflow.theme`), never sent to the server, and is not part of the case. Dark stays the default and is what a new browser, an unreadable stored value or blocked storage gives. Text, panels and borders follow `data-theme` through CSS; what is painted to a canvas cannot read a CSS variable, so a hex palette (`color/palette.ts`, kept equal to `tokens.css` by a test) is chosen by the current theme, and the graph and the timeline draw again when it changes. Spec 02 section 10.4 is untouched: an exported chart still defaults to light whatever the analyst is working in.

Not decided here. The map's basemap is not made theme-aware (it keeps its own styling in both themes). The Timeline's light appearance and the Sigma label colour in light have not been looked at by the owner. Judgement counts for a folded group: a member hidden inside a folded group shows no badge, and the node standing in for the group shows its own count only, not the group's total. Whether the group should show the total is for the owner to say.

Consequences. Keyboard: the Ranking and Communities section buttons and the theme button are ordinary buttons reached by Tab and pressed by Enter; `keyboard/metrics-panel.spec.ts` and `keyboard/top-bar.spec.ts` prove them, and `keyboard/keyboard.spec.ts` proves the badge, the three-step draw (and its large-result prompt) and the repaint on a theme change. `live/scenario-a-a12-a15.spec.ts` presses `Ranking` first (changed, not run: it needs the seeded stack). What a unit test cannot judge is how it looks: the owner should look at the badge, the closed Metrics panel and the light theme.


## ADR-071 — Telling nodes apart, a right-click menu that names its node and closes, and a search hint and Filters panel laid over the page

Status: accepted 3 October 2026 (found by the owner on the Enron case; no choice among options was needed).

Context. On the Enron case the owner selected two addresses through the search box and saw two small unlabelled squares, a right-click menu that stayed open when clicked away from, and no way to say which node was which. Separately, the one-line top bar grew a second line as soon as the search hint "Showing the first 10; more match. Keep typing to narrow." appeared, and again when the Filters panel opened. The owner also said the light and dark button was found "almost by mistake", and that the large-expansion prompt "appears randomly".

Decision.

1. **Labels.** A view of 40 nodes or fewer (`SMALL_VIEW_LABEL_LIMIT`) names every node whatever the zoom or the node's links. A node that is selected, under the pointer or on a found path is always named, in any view. The zoom rule in spec 02 section 1.1 is unchanged for a larger view with nothing selected.
2. **The node menu** is headed with the node's type and name (`Endpoint: jeff.dasovich@enron.com`, also its accessible name) and closes on a click anywhere outside it as well as on Escape. A click inside it does not close it.
3. **The search hint** ("more match") is laid over the page under the box, not part of the bar, and fades after four seconds (`SEARCH_HINT_MS`). It stays in the page for a screen reader. Only that nudge fades: "No match starts with that." and "Suggestions are unavailable." are answers and stay while the typed text stands. A new answer brings the hint back.
4. **The Filters panel** is laid over the page under the search box (it no longer pushes the bar down). While it is open it can cover the hint; only the order of the two is decided (the panel is on top).
5. **The light and dark button** is a worded button (`Light`, with the sun glyph) drawn like its neighbours, not a bare 28-pixel glyph. Any button with `aria-pressed="true"` (this one, and Graph, Map and Watches) now shows it: brass border and text on a raised surface. Before, none of them showed which was on.
6. **The large-expansion prompt** now names the node and the relationship being expanded and, when the size could not be counted, says nothing has been added. It was never random: it opens on a double-click on a node, on Enter with the canvas itself focused, on choosing a relationship in the node menu and on "Expand" by depth, and it opens whenever the size could not be counted (spec 02 and `expansionGate.ts`: not knowing is a reason to ask). On the Enron store the count calls do not answer, so every such gesture asks. The cause of the failed counts is not known (see below).

Not decided here. Why `/expand/preview` fails or does not answer on the large Enron store (the node menu's counts stay `(...)` and the prompt says `count unavailable`); a suspect is the parked lookup cost of ADR-058 Amendment 9, but nothing measured says so. The 40, the four seconds and the earlier crowding constants are first guesses to be tuned by looking at real views.

Consequences. `nodeAttributes.test.ts` (labels), `RadialMenu.test.tsx` (title and outside click), `GlobalSearch.test.tsx` (the hint fades; errors do not), `topBarStyle.test.ts` (the hint and panel are laid over the page; a pressed button looks pressed), `ThemeToggle.test.tsx` and `LargeExpansionPrompt.test.tsx` hold the units; `keyboard/keyboard.spec.ts` (small view named; menu named and closed by a click elsewhere) and `keyboard/top-bar.spec.ts` (the bar stays one line with the hint and with Filters open; the hint fades) hold the browser behaviour. The right-click-menu browser case was written after the fix, so it was not shown red; its behaviour was shown red at unit level. How any of it looks has not been judged by the owner.


## ADR-072 — The light and dark choice reaches every page of a deployment, through a cookie

Status: accepted 3 October 2026 (the owner asked for it in a comment on the verification walkthrough, after seeing the launcher's welcome page and the sign-in page stay dark; the cookie approach was put to the owner and confirmed).

Context. ADR-070 made the Glass light or dark and kept the choice in the page's own storage. A deployment is several pages, each on its own port of one host: the Glass, the launcher's welcome page (`make launch`), Keycloak's sign-in page, and the setup harness. All of them take their colours from `tokens.css`, which already has both ramps, but each started dark and none read a choice, and a browser keeps a page's storage per port so the Glass could not hand its choice on.

Decision.

1. The choice is also kept in a cookie, `ospreyflow_theme`, holding only `light` or `dark`, with `Path=/`, a one-year life and `SameSite=Lax`. A cookie is kept per host, not per port, so a choice made on any page reaches the others. No server reads it. `localStorage` stays as the fallback where cookies are refused.
2. The Glass (`theme/theme.ts`) reads the cookie first, since another page may have changed it since, then its own storage; a choice found only in storage is written to the cookie so existing choices carry over. The setup harness uses the same module, applies the choice before it draws, and carries the same `Light` button in its rail.
3. The launcher's pages and Keycloak's sign-in page are not React. They carry one plain script, `harness/theme_cookie.js`: it puts the choice on the page before it is drawn (in the head, so there is no flash of dark) and adds the same `Light` button at the top right (a real button, `aria-pressed` when light, coloured only from tokens). The launcher puts it in its head inline (the main page and its small message pages); the Keycloak theme ships it as `js/osprey-theme.js` and names it in `theme.properties` (`scripts=`). One file, so the pages cannot differ.
4. The button on every page now reads `Light` and is drawn like its neighbours; pressed means light (ADR-071 item 5).

Not decided here. Anything off this host: the pages of a deployment reached by different host names (`localhost` against `127.0.0.1`, or a separate sign-in domain) do not share a cookie and so do not share the choice; making them do so would need a cookie `Domain` and is for a real deployment to decide. The cookie is sent to every port on the host with every request, including other local services (it holds only `light` or `dark`); that is accepted.

Consequences. `theme.test.ts` (cookie written, read first, migrated, ignored when unknown, survives refused cookies), `themeCookieSnippet.test.ts` (runs the shipped file in a page with a cookie jar, against `theme.ts`, so the two cannot disagree about the cookie; every token it uses exists), `SummaryRail.test.tsx` (the harness button), `test_launch.py` and `test_launch_sign_in.py` (the script is in the head of the welcome page and of the message pages) and `test_keycloak_theme.py` (the theme names the script and ships the shared file). **Not proved:** that Keycloak 26's `keycloak.v2` login theme actually loads a script named by `scripts=` in `theme.properties`. That is how Keycloak's own login themes name scripts, but nothing here ran it against a real Keycloak (CLAUDE.md rule 15: a fixture models what the dependency accepts, not what it refuses), so the sign-in page following the choice is to be checked by the owner on a real deployment. Also not run in a browser: the launcher's and Keycloak's own buttons (they are plain buttons and are tested in a page with a cookie jar, not by keyboard in a browser), and the setup harness's button by keyboard (its Playwright suite needs the real harness server).

## ADR-073 — The light and dark button names the theme a press switches to

Status: accepted 3 October 2026 (the owner looked at the launcher's welcome page after switching it to light and said the button should then say `Dark`).

Context. ADR-071 item 5 made the button a worded `Light` button whose brass, pressed look meant "light is on", and ADR-072 item 4 put the same button on every page. The words never changed, so on a light page it still said `Light`: the only cue to what a press would do was the pressed colour, which does not say what the button will do, and a screen reader heard a fixed name with a pressed state.

Decision.

1. On every page the button's words, accessible name and tooltip name the theme a press switches to: `Light` (sun glyph, name `Switch to the light theme`) while the page is dark, and `Dark` (moon glyph, name `Switch to the dark theme`) once it is light.
2. Because the words now change with the state, the button no longer carries `aria-pressed` and no longer takes the brass pressed look. It is drawn like its neighbours in both themes.
3. This replaces the "pressed means light" part of ADR-071 item 5 and ADR-072 item 4 and the accessible name `Light theme` in ADR-070 item 4. Nothing else in those records changes: the button is still a real button, still reached by Tab and pressed by Enter or Space, still beside the account, and the choice is still kept as ADR-070 and ADR-072 say.
4. Spec 02 section 2 is amended to say so.

Not decided here. Whether the other buttons that show a pressed state (Graph, Map, Watches, Communities) should be reworded in the same way: they name a view, not an action, so they are left as they are.

Consequences. `ThemeToggle.test.tsx`, `SummaryRail.test.tsx` and `themeCookieSnippet.test.ts` assert both wordings and the absence of `aria-pressed`; `keyboard/top-bar.spec.ts` proves the keyboard route and that the words change in a real browser. The unit tests were run red against the old button first; the browser test and the harness test were changed in the same step and not shown red separately.

## ADR-074 — The search box finds names and titles, and starts after two characters

Status: accepted 3 October 2026 (the owner asked, and chose both options below from a written choice).

Context. The type-ahead (ADR-059, ADR-061) looks at each entity type's declared identifiers and its `indexed` string properties. For a `Person` that was the NI, PNC and prison numbers only, so a family name found nothing; likewise an `Organisation`'s name and a `Document`'s title. The owner saw it on the Fixture Corp case: typing `QQ` (two characters, below the minimum) showed nothing and said nothing, and a name found no one. The verification walkthrough had told the owner to search by name, which could not work.

Decision.

1. The ontology (version 11) marks `indexed: true` on `Person.family_name`, `Person.given_names`, `Organisation.name` and `Document.title` (`Location.name` already was). The type-ahead's scope rule is unchanged, so no new flag was needed; the schema step creates an index for each.
2. A property marked `sensitivity` is never searchable, since matching a prefix against a masked value would let a reader who may not see it guess it. `tests/ontology/test_searchable_names.py` holds this for every entity type. `Person.aliases` is not searchable yet: it is a list, and the scope rule takes only single strings.
3. The exact search (`POST /v1/search`) also reads `indexed` properties, so it now matches a family name exactly too. That is the existing rule for `Location.name`, stated in the adapter.
4. The minimum is two characters (`SUGGEST_MIN_CHARS`, the route and the Glass), down from three. While one character is typed the box says `Type at least 2 characters to search.` and the line stays until the text changes.
5. Every recipe fixture pinned to ontology version 10 is bumped to 11; a recipe left at 10 is blocked until re-published (spec 09).

Not decided here. Searching list properties such as aliases; ranking exact over partial matches; whether a two-character prefix is too costly on the largest case (ADR-059's 300 ms threshold still applies and is unmeasured for names).

Consequences. After deploying, the case's data must be seen by the new indexes: the API creates them when the schema step runs (a restart). Names are matched case-sensitively by default; the Filters panel's Ignore case option applies. The walkthrough's name searches (`Volkov`, `Ring 0 Holdings`) work only after this is deployed.

**ADR-074 Amendment 1 — marking a property `indexed` must also reach the nodes already stored.** Found 3 October 2026, the day ADR-074 shipped: with ontology v11 running, a search for `Petrenko` found nothing although both Petrenko nodes were on screen. The store keeps an indexed property twice, inside `properties` and as its own top-level field, and the index, `search_nodes` and `suggest_nodes` read only the field; the copy is made when a node is written (`serialization.py`). ADR-074 changed the ontology and assumed that was enough. It reached only nodes written afterwards, so every case seeded before v11 had names that could not be searched. The decision's own Consequences said the walkthrough's name searches would work after a restart; that was wrong for existing data.

Decision. Applying a schema now fills, for every indexed text or enumerated property, the top-level field from the `properties` map on nodes and links where the field is missing and the map has a value (`UPDATE <type> SET <field> = properties.<field> WHERE <field> IS NULL AND properties.<field> IS NOT NULL`). It never replaces a field that is present. It runs on every schema apply, so it also repairs a field missing for any other reason, and changes nothing once none is. If ArcadeDB refuses it, the rest of the schema step still runs, the API starts, and the refusal is logged naming the type and property. Dates and numbers are not filled (nothing searches them and they need a conversion). `04_VAULT_BACKEND.md` §1.4 says so.

Consequences. The first start after this change scans each type that has an indexed text property once, and every later start scans it again to find nothing to fill; on a store of hundreds of thousands of nodes that is a cost at start-up that has not been measured. Shown red first with a stand-in client (`test_schema_backfill.py`, five cases, three red). **Not run against a real ArcadeDB:** whether it accepts the `UPDATE` with the nested read `properties.<field>` is the unproven part, and the live case (`test_applying_the_schema_makes_a_name_findable_on_a_node_written_before_it_was_indexed` in the graph conformance suite) is written but not run. Until the owner has seen the log line or the search work, name search on old data is unproven; re-running a seed writes the field the ordinary way and is the fallback.


**ADR-074 Amendment 2 — the back-fill of Amendment 1 matched nothing, and said nothing.** Found 3 October 2026, after the owner ran `make refresh` and `Petrenko` still found nothing. The API log held no refusal, and reading the store showed `family_name` empty on both Petrenko nodes while the `properties` map held the name. Cause: Amendment 1 found the nodes to fill with `WHERE <field> IS NULL`, and the field is indexed. On ArcadeDB 25.5.1 that condition returned 0 rows (while 463 Person nodes had no value), most likely because it is answered from the index, which has no entry for a missing value; that reason is an inference, the 0 rows are measured. The statement was valid, so it neither failed nor logged; Amendment 1's guard against a refusal could not see a statement that succeeds and does nothing. My own live case, which would have shown it, was written and not run.

Decision. The nodes to fill are found with `WHERE properties.<field> IS NOT NULL AND ifnull(<field>, '') = ''`, which cannot use the index. Run by the owner on the real store: 463 found, 463 updated, 0 left, and both Petrenko nodes carried their names. Everything else in Amendment 1 stands (never replaces a value; every schema apply; a refusal is logged by name; text and enumerated properties only).

Consequences. The `UPDATE ... SET <field> = properties.<field>` form is now proven on ArcadeDB 25.5.1 for the Person type. Because the condition cannot use the index, every schema apply scans each type that has an indexed text property; this was already so in Amendment 1's intent and is still unmeasured on a store of hundreds of thousands of nodes. The stand-in test now pins the form and fails if `IS NULL` returns (`test_a_missing_field_is_not_asked_for_with_is_null`). The conformance case remains unrun in the repository.

## ADR-075 — Analysts can keep notes on a link

Status: accepted 3 October 2026.

Context. The owner asked for "the functionality to add notes for links for the analyst", after selecting a link. Two choices were put to the owner and answered: who sees a note ("everyone who can see the link", recommended) and its shape ("several dated notes per link, plain text", recommended). The spec was silent: judgements cite nodes only because `GraphPort` has no `get_edge`, so there was no way to ask the graph whether one link is visible to one person.

Decision.

1. A **note** is plain text, 1 to 4,000 characters, attached to one link in one investigation, with its author and time. A link has several, newest first. Text is shown as text, never as markup. The model is `LinkNote` (`01_DOMAIN_MODEL.md` §5, generated to TypeScript).
2. **Who may read or write a note: whoever can see its link.** The question is answered by `WorkingSetService.visible_edge`, which reads the one link and its two ends from the investigation's working set and applies the same handling filter every list read applies: the link's own marking and both ends must clear the person's clearance, and the link must be in this investigation's working set. A link the person cannot see answers exactly as a link that does not exist (404 `link_not_found`), on list, add, edit and delete, so a refusal reveals nothing about a hidden link.
3. A note has **no marking of its own**. It takes the link's by never being shown to anyone the link is not shown to. If the link is later marked above a reader, that reader loses its notes at once.
4. **Only the author edits or removes a note.** The database statement names the author, so another person's note matches nothing; the service then says 404 for a note that is not there and 403 `note_not_yours` for someone else's (the author is already shown beside every note, so this leaks nothing).
5. Levels (ADR-052): reading notes needs Viewer; adding, changing and removing need Editor. The route table in `test_investigation_levels.py` has all four rows.
6. Stored in Postgres, table `link_notes`, keyed by case and link, created idempotently like the other control-plane stores. Never written to the graph. The audit record for add, edit and remove holds the link and note ids, never the text.
7. Glass: the Inspector's **Notes** section for a selected link (`02_GLASS_FRONTEND.md` §2). Add, list, edit and delete your own (delete asks first), all reachable by keyboard.

Not decided here. A count of notes drawn on a link (offered, not chosen: it was the later step); notes on nodes; including notes in an export (nothing exports them, so an export does not mention them and the withheld-item manifest does not count them); searching note text; a note whose text quotes something more sensitive than its link (the section says a note takes the link's marking and asks the analyst not to put in anything more sensitive); a retention rule.

Consequences. A note on a link is unreachable while the link is outside the working set (its nodes were tidied away or the link was never loaded) and comes back when the link does; nothing is deleted. A link that a different working set holds under the same id would show the same case's notes, but the case is part of every lookup, so notes never cross cases. The access rule is tested at both layers: the service against a stand-in store that refuses what Postgres refuses (`test_link_notes.py`, shown red by removing the visibility check: 6 of 23 fail), and the Postgres statements themselves (`test_link_notes_store.py`, owner-run). Not exercised by this session: the four routes over real HTTP with a real token, and the Glass against a real case (owner to check).


## ADR-076 — The analyst chooses which property names each type of node

Status: accepted 3 October 2026.

Context. A reviewer of the Fixture Corp walkthrough wrote that the display "show Volkov across all the nodes, this is very confusing": six people of one family were each drawn as "Volkov", because a node was named by its family name alone. The reviewer asked that the analyst be able to choose what labels an entity type. The spec was silent: `02_GLASS_FRONTEND.md` named no rule for what a node is called. Two choices were put to the owner and answered: where the choice is kept ("this browser only", recommended) and what can be chosen ("one property per type", recommended).

Decision.

1. Per entity type, the analyst may choose one property to name its nodes. The choice is kept in this browser's own storage under one key, never sent to the server, and is not part of the case, the same standing the theme has (ADR-070). Another browser or machine starts with the default; another analyst's view is not affected.
2. A `Labels` button on the canvas offers a picker for each type that has a node in view, listing `Default` and the type's identifiers and other properties. A sensitive property (`sensitivity: high`) and a list property are not offered. The panel says the choice is kept in this browser only.
3. The chosen property names the node on the canvas, in the search list, in the cluster explanation and in the expansion prompt (they share one function). A node with no value for the chosen property keeps its default name: a label is never blank.
4. The default for a person is now "Family, Given" (family name alone when there are no given names). Other types keep what they had: the normalised value, else the id.
5. A new keyboard action, `labels-menu-by-keyboard`, is registered and proved (rule 13).

Not decided here. A label built from several properties; a choice shared by everyone on a case, or kept per analyst on the server (both were offered and not chosen); labelling links; a default for types other than Person (an organisation still shows its id until the analyst chooses `name`); hiding a value on the canvas that the analyst may read in the Inspector.

Consequences. A name chosen here is drawn for anyone looking at the analyst's screen, which is why a sensitive property is never offered. Choices are per type name, so a type renamed in a later ontology version loses its choice silently and shows the default. The canvas redraws when a choice changes; that redraw is proved with the layout settled, because while the layout moves the renderer redraws every frame and would hide a missing one. Not exercised: the Glass against a real case (owner to check).

## ADR-077 — An expansion that adds nothing says so

Status: accepted 3 October 2026.

Context. A reviewer on the Fixture walkthrough (step 1.6) wrote that choosing any relationship from the right-click menu "shows the change in the inspector but nothing on the canvas", and doubted the test. Read from the code and the dataset, not reproduced live: the Fixture's neighbours were already drawn (six people linked to each other), so each expansion added nothing, and an expansion that added nothing said nothing. The Inspector change was the right-click selecting the node. The spec was silent on what an expansion that adds nothing should do.

Decision.

1. When the answer to an expansion contains no node and no link that is not already drawn, the Glass shows a notice beside the node. If a relationship type was chosen: "Nothing new: everything linked by <type> is already in view." If the node was expanded without a type: "Nothing new: everything linked to this node is already in view." If nothing came back at all: "No <type> links from this node." (or "No links from this node.").
2. The notice is not an error: it has the `status` role, no error colour, and is closed with `Escape` or its own button. A failed expansion keeps its alert.
3. Nothing is said when anything new is drawn, including a node that was not drawn before or a link between two drawn nodes.
4. A new keyboard action, `expand-with-nothing-new-says-so`, is registered and proved (rule 13).

Consequences. The Conduit returns every node and link it found, drawn or not, so the Glass compares against what is on screen before the delta is applied; afterwards everything would count as drawn. Not decided here: telling the analyst how many were already in view; hiding a relationship in the menu once its neighbours are all drawn (the count shown beside it comes from the server's preview, which counts the size after expansion). Not seen in a live Glass: owner to check against the Fixture.

## ADR-078 — The right-click menu is grouped and sits above the canvas

Status: accepted 3 October 2026.

Context. The owner, looking at the Glass: the right-click menu "looks very cluttered". It was one flat list of relationship types and actions with each count run on after its name, and the canvas's own labels and nodes were drawn over its top row because the menu had no stacking order. Three layouts were put to the owner and one was chosen: one tidy list (recommended).

Decision.

1. Right-click and `\` open the same list. The relationship types are under a **Show links** heading and every other entry under **Actions**; a hairline separates the groups. The count is its own element, in the secondary text colour, at the right edge.
2. The order of the entries, and so the keyboard order, does not change. A heading is not an entry: it is hidden from assistive technology and each group is exposed as a labelled `group`.
3. The menu has a stacking order of 40, the same as the context menu, so it is drawn above the canvas.
4. The ring layout stays in the component but nothing opens it; right-click had already stopped using it (3 October 2026, the ring overlapped its own labels).

Consequences. No new keyboard action: the existing cases still prove every entry. The count beside a relationship is the server's preview of the size after expansion, not how many it would add (unchanged, and still to be fixed). Not seen in a live Glass: owner to check; checked in the harness in both themes.

## ADR-079 — A type of node has an icon: the ontology's default, and the analyst's own

Status: accepted 3 October 2026.

Context. The owner asked that icons can be associated with nodes by entity type. Two questions were put and answered: an icon is a glyph inside the existing shape (recommended), not a replacement for it, because shape is the colour-independent carrier of type that `02_GLASS_FRONTEND.md` §4 requires; and the icon is fixed by the ontology, with the analyst also able to define their own (the owner changed the answer from "analyst picks" and then asked for both, as "load icons by default but also allow the analyst to select their own icons or image thumbnails").

Decision.

1. `EntityTypeDef` gains an optional `icon`, one of twenty names held as a closed list in `ontology.schema.json`. The loader refuses any other name. Every type of the default ontology has one (Person: person, Endpoint: phone, Device: device, Location: pin, Organisation: building, Event: calendar, Document: document, Vehicle: vehicle, Asset: box). The ontology version stays 11: nothing a recipe writes, an index or an adapter reads has changed, and moving it would flag every published recipe as stale for a change that only affects how a node looks.
2. The Glass holds a drawing for each name, made for this project from plain shapes (no download, no licence). A test pins the Glass's list equal to the ontology schema's.
3. An `Icons` control beside `Labels` lets the analyst choose, per type in view: the default, another built-in drawing, none, or a picture of their own from a file. A picture must be a png, jpeg, webp or gif of up to 5 MB; an SVG is refused because it can carry scripts and links. It is cut to its middle square, drawn at 64 units and kept as a data address; a picture still too large to keep small is refused with a sentence saying so.
4. The choice is kept in this browser's own storage under one key, never sent to the server, and is not part of the case, the same standing the theme (ADR-070) and the label choice (ADR-076) have. A picture is only ever drawn from a data address that passes a strict check (a raster, base64, and nothing else), because it is placed inside an SVG.
5. The icon is drawn inside the node's own picture (shape, fill and provenance stroke are unchanged), in white or near-black, whichever is further from the fill. A picture is cut to the shape, with the provenance outline drawn over it. A dimmed or filtered-out node fades its icon.
6. A new keyboard action, `icons-menu-by-keyboard`, and `icon-picture-from-file` are registered and proved (rule 13). The picture case reads the canvas's pixels, so it proves the image reaches the screen and not only the node's stored attribute.

Not decided here: a picture or icon per node rather than per type; icons in the search list, the Inspector or a legend; sharing a choice between analysts or keeping it on the server (the picture is only in this browser); a larger node when it has an icon (nodes are 6 to 16 pixels across at the usual zoom, so an icon is legible only when zoomed in); more than twenty drawings, or an ontology naming one that is not on the list.

Consequences. A picture an analyst chooses is drawn for anyone looking at their screen, and would be drawn in an image export of the canvas (not checked); nothing checks what the picture shows, which is the analyst's responsibility, as for a typed label (ADR-076). A browser that will not store the picture (a full or blocked store) still shows it for the page and says so. Choices are per type name, so a type renamed in a later ontology loses its choice and shows the default. Not seen in a live Glass: owner to check. Observed, not changed: in the harness a node drawn large shows a coloured square behind its round shape; that predates icons and is recorded in the build plan.

## ADR-080 — A right-click menu on a link: fold a match into one node, confirm or refute it, change a link, and keep the history

Status: accepted 3 October 2026 (the owner asked in the Fixture doc thread for options on a same-as link, then confirmed the design: "yes this sounds right"; for other links, "change the link and add notes" with "an audit history" always; and "yes agreed" to a change covering both the type and the details, with a required reason and the old value kept).

Context. A link could be selected (ADR-064), hidden, and noted (ADR-075), but there was no menu on it, no way to look at a same-as match as the one entity it claims to be, and no way for an analyst to correct a link at all: the only analyst writes on a link's pair were the two manual assertions on nodes (`resolution/link`, `resolution/split`), written with no stated reason. The spec had `GraphPort.supersede_edge` (`01_DOMAIN_MODEL.md` §8.2) but nothing that called it from an analyst's hand.

Decision.

1. **A menu on every drawn link.** Right-click on a link (the click finds the nearest link within 6 pixels, ADR-064) or, with a link selected, `\`, opens a list titled `TYPE: A ↔ B`, drawn like the node menu (ADR-078). Reached by keyboard: `L` selects a focused node's link, `\` opens the menu.
2. **A same-as link offers:** *Collapse into one node* (then *Expand*), *Confirm as the same*, *Mark as not the same*, *Explain this link*, *Add a note*, *Hide link*. A not-the-same link offers only a note and hiding: it is a judgement the analyst made, and undoing it is a new judgement, not an edit. **Any other link offers:** *Change link…*, *Show change history*, *Add a note*, *Hide link*.
3. **Collapse is a view, never a write** (rule 6). It folds into a Group Node, by the machinery Communities use (ADR-066): the whole resolution cluster when both ends are in one, otherwise the two ends. Nothing is merged or stored; the fold is lost when the tab is reloaded. Expand is in the link's menu while the link is drawn; because a link inside a folded group is not drawn, a Group Node's own menu also has *Expand group*, and double-click and `G` still open it.
4. **Confirm and Mark as not the same ask why first.** The box needs a reason (Control+Enter or its button; Escape cancels) and the reason is recorded as the justification on the existing audit row for the assertion. The routes' `reason` field is optional so existing callers keep working; the Glass always sends one.
5. **Change link… is the Inspector's form**, offered for a link of any type other than same-as and not-the-same: the type (only types the ontology allows between the two ends' entity types, never a same-as type), the properties that type declares, the validity period, the number of records behind it, and a **required reason** of up to 1,000 characters. A change that changes nothing is refused. A link cannot be changed into, or out of, a same-as type: those are confirmed or marked, because the resolution engine's links and its clusters must not disagree.
6. **A change is a supersede, not an edit.** `GraphPort.supersede_edge` keeps the old link (marked `superseded_by`), writes a new link with the revision one higher and a new id, keeps the marking and both ends, and records provenance as asserted, sourced `manual:change:<old id>`. The analyst's notes on the old link move to the new one in the same step. The working set learns of it by a new delta, `replace_edge`, so every open screen swaps the link at once.
7. **History is always kept.** Every write from this menu (change, confirm, mark as not the same) writes an `audit_log` row naming the analyst and the reason. Because the audit stream has no read path, a change also writes a row to a readable Postgres table, `link_changes`: who, when, why, and the type, properties, validity period and record count before and after, linking the new link to the one it replaced. `GET .../links/{edge}/history` follows those links back through every earlier version (bounded at 100 steps, and it says so when it stops). The Inspector shows it as *Change history*.
8. **Access (rules 3 and 4).** Both new routes answer exactly as link notes do: whoever can see the link, by `WorkingSetService.visible_edge`, with one 404 `link_not_found` for a link that is missing and one the person may not see, and history is read only through that check. Levels (ADR-052): history needs Viewer, change needs Editor.

Not decided here. Whether a change should also be a step in the investigation's History (it is not now: restoring an earlier step could put a replaced link back in the working set, which the owner should know); recomputing the link's `weight` in the working set at once (it keeps the old figure until the link is read again from the graph); changing or deleting a same-as or not-the-same link by hand; undoing a change (the way back is another change, and both are in the history); a fold that survives a reload or is shared with other analysts; a count of changes drawn on a link.

Consequences. New: `services/api/link_changes.py`; routes `POST` and `GET` under `links/{edge}/change|history`; the `replace_edge` delta in the hand-kept protocol (`working_set/models.py`, `workingset/models.ts`); `LinkNoteStore.rekey`. Tests that would fail if an invariant broke: `test_link_changes.py::test_changing_a_link_the_principal_cannot_see_is_indistinguishable_from_missing` and `::test_reading_the_history_of_a_link_the_principal_cannot_see_is_indistinguishable` (rules 3 and 4); `::test_same_as_and_not_the_same_links_are_not_changed_here` and `::test_a_link_cannot_be_changed_into_a_same_as_link` (rule 6); `::test_the_reason_is_required`; `::test_the_change_is_recorded_with_who_when_why_and_old_and_new_values`; `::test_notes_on_the_old_link_follow_it_to_the_new_one`; `::test_a_failure_in_the_graph_leaves_the_working_set_and_history_untouched`; `test_link_change_routes.py::test_a_change_is_audited_with_the_reason_and_the_old_and_new_values`; `test_investigation_levels.py` (the two new rows); the Glass unit tests for the menu entries, the fold, the form, the history list and the working-set swap; and in a browser `keyboard/link-menu.spec.ts` (`LINK_MENU_ACTIONS`) and `keyboard/link-change.spec.ts` (`LINK_CHANGE_ACTIONS`), which reach every entry by keyboard (rule 13). Also changed while proving it by keyboard: a menu or box that closes now returns keyboard focus to the canvas (it was left on the page body), and focusing the canvas no longer picks a node folded away or drops a selected link. **Not run here:** `test_link_changes_store.py` and the new rekey case in `test_link_notes_store.py` need a real Postgres (owner-run); the new routes over HTTP against a real graph store (ArcadeDB's `supersede_edge` is covered by the existing conformance suite, not by a run from this change); and the menu in a live Glass. The unit tests for the access refusals use a stand-in that refuses what the real check refuses, but they were not shown red against a store with the check removed.

### ADR-080, Amendment 1 (3 October 2026) — a fold made from a same-as link is opened when the resolution changes

Context. The owner walked the Fixture Corp case after ADR-080 and reported, at "Back to Balanced", that "this is now only showing 2 nodes where previously there were more", and that Explain cluster "doesn't seem to be working" on the next step. Reproduced in the browser harness: a fold made with *Collapse into one node* is kept by the canvas as its own list of groups, and that list was pruned only when a member left the view. A `reproject` delta (the slider moved, or a match was confirmed or refused) changes the clusters the fold was made from, but the fold stayed, so after Strict, Broad and back to Balanced the five Volkov nodes stayed one Group Node and the view showed fewer nodes than the resolution says it should. Hidden inside a Group Node, the pair of step 2.8 could not be selected either.

Decision. When a `reproject` delta lands, every fold made from a same-as link is opened again and the analyst is told once ("The resolution changed, so the nodes you collapsed are shown again."). Folds made by Communities are not touched: they are worked out afresh from the links in view. The analyst can fold again from the link. ADR-080 item 3 (collapse is a view, never a write) stands; this only ends the fold's life earlier.

Not decided here. Whether a fold should be re-made for the new cluster instead of being opened (not done: the new cluster may be different people).

Consequences. Changed: `canvas/GlassCanvas.tsx` (one effect keyed on the last `reproject`). The test that would fail if a stale fold survived: `keyboard/link-menu.spec.ts`, "Moving the resolution slider opens a same-as fold", registry id `moving-the-resolution-slider-opens-a-same-as-fold`; shown red before the change (the fold stayed at 3 grouped nodes). Explain cluster itself was not found faulty in the harness (its keyboard case passes); whether it also failed live for another reason is for the owner to confirm after `make refresh`.

## ADR-081 — Every relationship type declares whether it is Direct or Probabilistic, and how it is drawn; analysts may propose new types

Status: accepted 3 October 2026 (owner's choices); build staged, nothing built yet.

Context. The owner, looking at how probabilistic matches appear in the Fixture Corp case, asked that every relationship type declare whether it is **Direct** (a direct, established database link) or **Probabilistic**; that every declaration may carry a line colour and thickness; that a probabilistic match may only ever be drawn dotted; and, earlier, that an analyst can change a link's type and define a new type when none fits. Three choices were put and answered: the classification lives on **both** the type and the link; new types are **proposed by an analyst and promoted by an administrator**; a Direct line is **solid only**. The owner added that the Ingest Studio must load Direct types from the load schema itself (a device-to-CDR relation is Direct; so is ownership where an evidential record is loaded), and that a probabilistic relationship is either statistically derived or declared by an analyst. Today a type has no such setting (`EdgeTypeDef` in `packages/schemas/domain.py`), every link is drawn in one border colour with thickness from its weight, and dotted lines exist only on node borders (provenance).

Decision.

1. **`basis` is required on every relationship type**: `direct` or `probabilistic`. An ontology that omits it is refused at load (the ontology JSON Schema and `EdgeTypeDef`), so there is no unclassified type. Every current type is declared `direct` except `SAME_AS`, which is `probabilistic`.
2. **A link has a basis too.** It takes its type's basis. A link of a Direct type may be marked probabilistic (statistically derived, or declared by an analyst with a reason); a link of a Probabilistic type is always probabilistic. A link is never promoted to Direct by a person: Direct means a loaded record stands behind it.
3. **Who writes each basis.** A relationship written by the Ingest Studio from the source's own schema (a column pairing, a key, a record the source holds) is Direct, and a recipe that names a Probabilistic type is refused at validation (rule 8 stands: no expression language). The resolution engine writes Probabilistic links only. An analyst who asserts a link states its basis in the form; there is no default. Confirming a `SAME_AS` link (ADR-080) leaves it probabilistic: a person has judged the match, no database record has linked the two. Rule 5 stands.
4. **Drawing.** The line style is not authored, it follows the basis: Direct is always solid, Probabilistic is always dotted. A declaration may carry a **colour** (a name from the closed list in `design/tokens.css`, never a free colour: no colour outside the tokens) and a **thickness** (a whole number, 1 to 5). With neither, today's border colour and weight-based width apply. A link's own basis decides its style, so a probabilistic link of a Direct type is dotted in the type's colour.
5. **New relationship types.** When none fits, an Editor **proposes** one from the change form: a name, the entity types at each end, directed or not, basis, colour and thickness. It is usable at once in that investigation only, is labelled analyst-defined, is kept in the control-plane store (not in the shared ontology, not in the graph), and is audited with the analyst and a reason. An analyst-proposed type is **probabilistic** until an administrator reclassifies it. An **administrator promotes** a proposal: promotion is an ontology change, a new ontology version through the existing schema step, and is the only way a type enters the shared ontology. An administrator may also reject one.
6. **The ADR-080 change form** shows each offered type's basis and style, and offers *Define a new type…*.

Not decided here. Which role is the administrator (ADR-052 has Viewer, Editor and Owner of an investigation, none of them an ontology administrator); whether an analyst-proposed type may declare Direct when the administrator has not yet seen a loader that backs it (this ADR says it may not, and that is my reading of the owner's words, to be confirmed); how a declared thickness combines with a link's weight; what happens to links of a type that is later rejected; the basis of `NOT_SAME_AS`, which is an analyst's judgement and is drawn as today.

Consequences. When built: `EdgeTypeDef` and `OntologySchema` gain `basis`, `colour`, `thickness`; `Edge` gains a per-link `basis`; the TypeScript types are regenerated (drift is a build failure); the ontology YAML and its JSON Schema change; the Ingest Studio's recipe validator checks the basis; a control-plane table for proposals and the routes for propose, list and promote (each with an access-control test, rules 3 and 4, and levels under ADR-052); the Glass draws dotted links. Sigma's stock edge programs draw solid lines; whether the installed version has a dotted one is not yet checked and is the first thing to find out, because the drawing may need a custom edge program. Tests that would fail if an invariant were broken: an ontology without `basis` is refused; a probabilistic link is drawn dotted whatever colour its type declares; a Direct link is never drawn dotted; a recipe naming a Probabilistic type is refused; a Viewer cannot propose, an Editor cannot promote, and a proposal from one investigation is invisible in another. Build in four steps, each its own commit: (A) `basis`, colour and thickness on types and the drawing; (B) the per-link basis; (C) proposals and promotion; (D) the Ingest Studio's rule.

### ADR-080, Amendment 2 (3 October 2026) — correction: the nodes missing after the slider were not a fold

Context. Amendment 1 above said a stale same-as fold explained the owner's report at step 2.7 ("only 2 nodes where previously there were more") and that, with the pair hidden in a Group Node, step 2.8 could not select it. The owner's screenshots then showed no Group Node at any stop: six people at Balanced, three at Strict, two at Broad, and two again on returning to Balanced, with the status bar not counting folded nodes. Amendment 1 named a real fault, reproduced and fixed, but not the one the owner saw. That explanation was wrong for this report and is withdrawn as its cause.

What the owner saw. The cluster drawing (`02_GLASS_FRONTEND.md` §1.1, "Collapse (B9)") puts every node of a cluster at the cluster's anchor. The code that was meant to give a node its own place back when its cluster splits skipped any node that had become its own cluster, so after a split the nodes stayed stacked on the old anchor. Each move of the slider stacked more of them, and returning to Balanced did not separate them: two points on screen for six people. The specification already said a node returns to its own place; the code did not.

Decision. A node that is no longer drawn on another's place goes back to where it was before it was joined, and the layout then runs so each node has a place of its own (ids that differ in one character scatter to nearly the same point). The test that would fail: `keyboard/resolution-slider.spec.ts` ("people matched as one are drawn together; a split puts each back in a place of its own"), shown red before the change (the people stayed together after a split) and green after. Amendment 1's change (same-as folds open when the resolution changes) stands as a separate fault.

Not decided here, not reproduced. The owner's first screenshot, at Balanced and before the slider was touched, shows six separate people although the specification expects the Mikael and Mikhail pair and the identical pair to be merged at Balanced. It may be that nodes drawn into the view arrive without their cluster until the first `reproject`. I have not reproduced it; the owner is asked to repeat 2.1 and 2.2 after this change and say what the first view shows.

## ADR-082 — The side panel and the timeline can be hidden, and the side panel can open to the whole work area

Status: accepted 3 October 2026.

Context. The owner asked that the Inspector and the timeline be collapsible, and that the Inspector be able to expand fully "so that the analyst can use the query function fully". The right-hand column holds the Inspector, the metrics and the query builder in a fixed 320 pixels; the timeline is fixed at 252 pixels.

Decision.

1. The right-hand column is framed by `SidePanelFrame`, with three states: **normal** (320 pixels, as before), **collapsed** (a narrow strip with one button to bring it back) and **full** (it covers the whole work area, over the canvas, which keeps its size so nothing in the view moves). Buttons: *Hide*, *Full width*, *Normal width*, *Show the inspector*.
2. The timeline is framed by `BottomPanelFrame`: a title row with *Hide* / *Show*; hidden, the work area takes its height.
3. Hidden contents stay mounted, so a half-written query, the timeline's brush and playback are as they were when the panel is shown again.
4. This is the layout of one browser tab: nothing is stored or sent, and each panel opens in its normal state on reload.

Not decided here. Remembering a choice between sessions (not done: it would need a place to keep a per-analyst setting); a hide shortcut key; a drag handle to set the width.

Consequences. New `src/layout/PanelFrames.tsx` with unit tests; `App.tsx` uses both frames; the keyboard registry `PANEL_FRAME_ACTIONS` and `keyboard/panel-frames.spec.ts` prove the three buttons by keyboard (rule 13). Spec 02 §2 states the behaviour.

## ADR-083 — Two more layouts: a force-directed tree and clustered bubbles

Status: accepted 3 October 2026.

Context. The owner asked for the force-directed tree and the clustered bubbles of two Observable D3 notebooks to be brought into the Glass. Four choices were put and answered: they are **two new entries in the Layout menu**; the tree is rooted on **the selected node, else the most linked**; the bubbles group by **a key the analyst picks**; and **no new packages** are added (the Glass already has its own force layout, `forceLayout.ts`). The result resembles the examples, it does not reproduce them.

Decision.

1. **Force-directed tree** (`layoutModes.ts`, `tree`). A shortest-path tree is grown from the root (the selected node, otherwise the most linked); each piece of the graph the root does not reach is rooted on its own most linked node, so no node is left out. The tree starts as a radial tree (repeatable: the same graph settles the same way) and the existing force layout then settles it, with only the tree's links pulling. Above 1,000 nodes the force step is skipped and the radial tree stands, so the layout is never refused. Links that are not part of the tree stay in the view, drawn faint (never removed, rule 2); selecting one draws it as any selected link.
2. **Clustered bubbles** (`bubbles`). One bubble for each group, its nodes packed inside it, the bubbles packed against one another without overlapping, the largest in the middle. A circle with the group's name and size is drawn round each. The key is chosen in a second menu beside Layout, **Bubbles by**: *Entity type* (the default) or *Community* (found from the links in view, whether or not Communities is switched on; nodes in no community form one bubble, "Not in a community"). The size beside a bubble counts every node, including nodes the engine has matched as one and so draws on one place.
3. Both are views of the working set, like the other layouts: they change where nodes are drawn, never what is stored or what is in the view (rules 2 and 6), and switching layout never refetches.
4. The choice is kept in the browser tab only, as the other layouts are.

Not decided here. Grouping by resolution cluster (the layout works on one node for each cluster, so every cluster would be a bubble of one); a bubble the analyst can fold into a Group Node (Communities offers that already); drawing the tree with the root at the top; animating the bubbles' packing.

Consequences. Changed: `canvas/layoutModes.ts` (`tree`, `bubbles`, `treeLinkKeys`, `enclosingCircle`, `linkKey`), `canvas/LayoutMenu.tsx` (the *Bubbles by* choice), new `canvas/BubbleOverlay.tsx`, and `canvas/GlassCanvas.tsx` (the faint links and the bubble circles).
